questions.stem: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?
options: A static variable declared inside a function
An array of integers declared inside a function
A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

solutionDiagram.alt: Memory layout of a C program: the stack holds locals and return addresses, the heap holds malloc blocks, the static data segment holds globals and static variables; each option is tied to its region.

steps.title: The regions of a running C program
steps.body: A C program's memory is split into regions, and the region of an object is fixed by how and when the object is created. The static (data) segment holds objects that live for the whole run: global variables and any variable declared static, even inside a function. The stack holds one frame for each active function call: its parameters, its ordinary (automatic) local variables, local arrays, and the return address saved by the call; the frame is discarded when the function returns. The heap holds blocks that the program asks for while it runs, with malloc, calloc or realloc; a block stays until free is called. The rule: storage follows the way the object was created, not where its name is visible.

steps.title: Place each option
steps.body: A static variable inside a function is visible only in that function but lives for the whole run, so it sits in the static segment. An array of integers declared inside a function is an automatic variable: it sits in the stack frame of the call. An array obtained from malloc is a block requested at run time, so it sits in the heap. The return address is saved by the call so the function knows where to resume: it sits on the stack. Only option C is in the heap.

shortcut.body: Heap means malloc, calloc or realloc, and nothing else in C creates heap memory. Scan the options for one of those calls: only (C) has it. The others are a static (data segment) and two stack items, which takes about 20 seconds.

traps.text: A static local variable is easy to mistake for dynamic storage because it keeps its value between calls. It is allocated once for the whole run in the static segment; no malloc is involved.

A local array is "allocated" when the function is entered, which sounds like run-time allocation. It is an automatic variable placed in the call's stack frame, however large it is, and it vanishes on return.
The return address belongs to the function-call mechanism: the call saves it on the stack so that execution can resume after the return. It is never part of the heap.

recognize.clues: The words "stored in heap" together with a list mixing a static local, a local array, a malloc block and a return address: each option names a different creation mechanism.
recognize.contrast: A static local looks dynamic because it keeps its value between calls, but it is allocated once in the static segment. Heap storage always comes from a library allocation call and must be released with free.

check.body: Test each region by lifetime. If the object vanishes when its function returns, it was on the stack, which removes the local array and the return address. If it exists before main starts and until the program ends, it is in the static segment, which removes the static local. What is left is the only object whose lifetime the program controls with free.

questions.stem:
Consider the following three ANSI-C programs, P1, P2, and P3.

Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Only P1 will compile without any error
Only P2 will compile without any error
Only P3 will compile without any error
All three programs P1, P2, and P3 will compile without any error

solutionDiagram.alt: Three panels: P1 declares a at file scope and again inside main, which is legal; P2 and P3 declare a twice inside the same block of main, which is a compile error.

steps.title: Scope, declaration and shadowing
steps.body: A declaration introduces a name, and the scope of the name is the part of the program where it can be used. A name declared outside every function has file scope; a name declared between braces has block scope, and the scope ends at the closing brace. The rule has two halves. Within one scope a name may be declared only once, whatever the types. A block may declare a name that already exists in an enclosing scope; the new variable then hides the outer one (shadowing) until the block ends.

steps.title: Check P1, P2 and P3
steps.body: P1: a = 5 is at file scope and a = 7 is in the block of main. These are two different scopes, so the inner declaration shadows the outer one: legal. P2: both a = 5 and a = 7 are declared in the same block of main, which is a redefinition of a: compile error. P3: again two declarations of a in one block; changing the type to float does not help, because C has no overloading, so the compiler reports a conflicting redefinition. A compiler run confirmed it: P1 compiled, P2 gave "redefinition of a", P3 gave "redefinition of a with a different type". Only P1 compiles, option A.

shortcut.body: For each program, look for the same name declared twice between the same pair of braces. P2 and P3 have it; P1 has the second a one scope deeper than the first. So only P1 compiles. Unsafe only if a program uses a macro or typedef that hides a second declaration.

traps.text: Reading "int a=5; int a=7;" as an assignment that replaces 5 by 7. The second line is a second declaration of a, not an assignment, so it is a redefinition error.
Thinking that a different type, float against int, makes the second a a different variable. In C a name has one meaning per scope, so the type changes nothing.
Assuming that any repeated name is shadowing. Shadowing needs an inner scope that is opened with braces; two declarations in the same block of main are one scope.

recognize.clues: Three short programs that each declare a twice, with one at file scope and two inside the same block, ask which compile: the test is where each declaration sits.
recognize.contrast: Shadowing, an inner scope reusing an outer name, is legal. Redefinition, two declarations in one scope, is an error, and a different type (int then float) does not make it shadowing.

check.body: Rename the second declaration of a to b in each program and recompile in your head. P2 and P3 now compile, because their error was two declarations of a in one block. P1 compiled before the rename and still does. Only P1 had no clash to begin with, which matches option A.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI-C program.

The output of this program is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: Assume that the program compiles and runs successfully.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three snapshots of the variables a, b, c and the pointer ptr: a becomes 20 through ptr, then a becomes 11 from b while ptr moves to c, then c becomes 20 minus 11, which is 9.

steps.title: Pointers in one rule
steps.body: A pointer variable holds the address of another variable. The expression &x is the address of x. The expression *p names the variable that p points to: reading *p gives that variable's value, and assigning to *p changes that variable. The operators * and & undo each other, so *(&b) is simply b. The rule for a trace: at each statement, know which variable every pointer points to, and treat *ptr as another name for that variable.

steps.title: Trace the statements
steps.body: Start with a = 5, b = 11, c = 20. ptr = &a makes ptr point to a. *ptr = c stores 20 into the variable ptr points to, so a = 20. ptr = &c makes ptr point to c. a = *(&b) copies b into a, so a = 11 (the 20 is overwritten). Then c = *ptr - a: *ptr is now c itself, so this is c = c - a = 20 - 11 = 9.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: printf prints the final value of c, which is 9. A compiled run printed 9, with a = 20 after the first store and a = 11 after the copy.

shortcut.body: Once ptr = &c has run, *ptr is just c, so the last line means c = c - a. The value of a is the last one written: a = *(&b) = b = 11. So c = 20 - 11 = 9.

traps.text: Answering 15: using a = 5 because a looks untouched. It was overwritten twice, first with 20 through ptr and then with 11, so a = 11 when c is computed.
Answering 0: stopping after *ptr = c (a = 20) and missing a = *(&b). Then c = 20 - 20 = 0. The statement a = *(&b) is a plain copy of b into a.

recognize.clues: Declarations of an int pointer and three ints, then a store through *ptr and a re-aim of ptr to c, ask for a final value: a pure trace of what each pointer currently names.
recognize.contrast: No arithmetic on the pointer itself happens here, only & and *. This is pointer aliasing, not pointer arithmetic over array elements.

check.body: Redo it as a table of (a, b, c) after each statement, starting from (5, 11, 20). After ptr=&a: (5, 11, 20). After *ptr=c: (20, 11, 20). After ptr=&c: (20, 11, 20). After a=*(&b): (11, 11, 20). The last line reads c as *ptr, so c becomes 20 - 11 and the table ends at (11, 11, 9).

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI-C function.

The maximum possible value that can be returned from this function is ____________. (answer in integer)

Note: Ignore syntax errors (if any) in the function.

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain of lengths: remainder 1 adds 1 and moves to 3m; from 3m the length goes 3m, 3m-1, 3m-3 and so on down to a length below 1, which returns 0; remainder 2 also moves to 3m. Only one plus one can occur.

steps.title: What a recursive call returns
steps.body: A recursive function returns a value built from the values of smaller calls. Here the base case, length below 1 or a negative index, returns 0, and every other call returns what its one recursive call returns, possibly plus 1. So the value of a call is the number of "1 +" branches taken along the single chain of calls until the base case. The length L = end + 1 - start decides which branch runs, so only L matters. The rule: follow how L changes along the chain and count the "1 +" steps.

steps.title: What each branch does to the length
steps.body: If L mod 3 = 0, the call is func(start+1, end): L becomes L - 1 and nothing is added. If L mod 3 = 2, the call is func(start+2, end): L becomes L - 2 and nothing is added. If L mod 3 = 1, the call is 1 + func(start, end-1): L becomes L - 1 and 1 is added. A remainder of 1 is the only branch that adds anything.

steps.title: Follow the chain
steps.body: From L = 3m the remainders go 0, then 2 (L = 3m - 1), then 0 again (L = 3m - 3), and so on: remainders 0 and 2 alternate and never produce a remainder of 1, so the chain ends at L below 1 with nothing added. From L = 3m + 2 the next length is 3m, again a chain with no addition. From L = 3m + 1 the call adds 1 and moves to L = 3m, which adds nothing more. So one "1 +" is the most any chain can collect. Example: func(0, 0) has L = 1 and returns 1 + func(0, -1) = 1 + 0 = 1. A brute-force run over every start and end from -3 to 59 gave a maximum of exactly 1.

shortcut.body: Only the remainder-1 branch adds 1, and it always leads to remainder 0, after which lengths go 0, 2, 0, 2 and never return to remainder 1. So at most one 1 is added: the maximum is 1, reached by func(0, 0).

traps.text: Answering 0 because the base case returns 0 and the other two branches pass the value on. The branch for remainder 1 adds 1 on the way back, and func(0, 0) shows it returns 1.
Expecting the remainder to cycle 1, 0, 2, 1, ... so that 1 is added every third step and the answer grows with the length. The remainders after a 1 go 0, 2, 0, 2, so the addition happens only once.

recognize.clues: The question asks for a maximum over all inputs of a function that makes a single recursive call chosen by a remainder: follow the one chain and count the additions.
recognize.contrast: This is not a recurrence for running time (recursion-recurrences): the function's return value is traced, not its cost.

check.body: Test small cases by hand. Length 1 gives 1 plus a base case. Length 2 jumps to length 0 and returns 0. Length 3 goes to 2, then 0. Length 4 adds 1 and lands on 3, which adds nothing. Length 7 behaves like length 4. None of these exceeds the value found for length 1, which agrees with the chain argument.

questions.stem:
Consider the following program in C:

The output of the program is _________. (answer in integer)

Note: Assume that the program compiles and runs successfully.

solutionDiagram.alt: The frame of func holds the parameter i = 9 and j; the block of the if declares a new i that counts up to 10 and hides the outer i, but printf is outside the block and prints the outer i, 9.

steps.title: Two variables with one name
steps.body: A parameter is a variable that belongs to the function call, and it starts with a copy of the argument: here func(9, 10) gives the parameter i the value 9 and j the value 10. A block is the code between { and }. If a block declares a name that already exists outside it, the block gets a new, separate variable with that name, which hides the outer one until the closing brace and is destroyed there. The rule: a name in printf means the innermost variable of that name that is visible at the place where it is written.

steps.title: Run func(9, 10)
steps.body: The test i < j is 9 < 10, true, so the block runs. Inside it, int i = 0 creates a new i. The loop runs while this new i is below 10: each pass adds 2 to j and 1 to the new i, so after 10 passes the new i is 10 and j is 10 + 20 = 30. The block then ends and the new i disappears. The call printf("%d", i) is after the block, where i means the parameter, which was never changed: it prints 9.

shortcut.body: Spot int i = 0 inside the if block: the loop only touches that inner i. The printf is outside the block, so it prints the outer i, which still holds the 9 that was passed in. No need to count the loop passes.

traps.text: Answering 10: reading printf as seeing the loop variable that finished at 10. The loop variable belongs to the block and no longer exists when printf runs.
Answering 30 or 0: 30 is the final value of j, not of i, and 0 is the start value of the inner i. The printed variable is the parameter i, which is 9.

recognize.clues: A local int i declared inside the if block with the same name as the parameter, and a printf after the block: the loop runs on a different variable from the one printed.
recognize.contrast: Parameter passing (parameter-passing) asks whether the caller sees changes; here the caller is irrelevant, the question is only which i the printf names.

check.body: Rename the inner variable to k in your head and rewrite the loop with k. The loop then clearly never touches i, and printf(i) prints the parameter exactly as it arrived. The number of loop passes and the growth of j are irrelevant to the printed value.

questions.stem:
Consider the recursive functions represented by the following code segment:

The smallest positive integer n for which foo(n) returns 5 is ______. (answer in integer)

Note: Ignore syntax errors (if any) in the function.

solutionDiagram.alt: The chain 65536, 16, 4, 2, 1 where each arrow is bar, the floor of log base 2, with foo values 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 below the numbers.

steps.title: What bar and foo compute
steps.body: Integer division n/2 drops the fraction. bar(n) counts how many halvings it takes to bring n down to 1, so bar(n) is floor(log2 n); for example bar(8) = 3 and bar(15) = 3. foo(n) is 1 plus foo of that count, so foo(n) is the number of values in the chain n, bar(n), bar(bar(n)), ... that ends at 1. The rule: foo(n) = k exactly when the chain from n down to 1 has k numbers.

steps.title: Work backwards from foo = 5
steps.body: Which x have foo(x) = 1? Only x = 1. foo(x) = 2 needs bar(x) = 1, so x is 2 or 3. foo(x) = 3 needs bar(x) in {2, 3}, so x runs from 4 to 15. foo(x) = 4 needs bar(x) in 4..15, so x runs from 16 to 65535. foo(x) = 5 needs bar(x) at least 16, so x is at least 2^16. The smallest values for foo = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are 1, 2, 4, 16, 65536: each is 2 raised to the previous one.

steps.title: Check the boundary
steps.body: bar(65536) = 16 and foo(16) = 4, so foo(65536) = 5. One step below, bar(65535) = 15 and foo(15) = 3, so foo(65535) = 4. A run over all n up to 70000 printed 65536 as the first n with foo(n) = 5, so the answer is 65536.

shortcut.body: The smallest n with foo(n) = k is a tower of 2s: 1, 2, 4, 16, 65536. Each term is 2 to the power of the one before, because the smallest x with floor(log2 x) = m is 2^m. Five terms give 65536. Unsafe only if the question asked for the largest n.

traps.text: Answering 32: reading foo(n) = 5 as "five halvings", so 2^5. But foo takes the logarithm and then recurses on that small number, so the argument shrinks far faster than halving. foo(32) is only 4.
Answering 16 or 65535: 16 is the smallest n with foo(n) = 4, one level short, and 65535 is the largest n with foo(n) = 4. The next jump happens exactly at 2^16.

recognize.clues: Two mutually dependent recursive functions with n/2 and a request for the smallest n giving a particular value: invert the recursion level by level.
recognize.contrast: This is not a divide-and-conquer recurrence for running time; bar and foo are evaluated for their return values, and the logarithm appears as the value, not the cost.

check.body: Use a second route: count the chain of exact powers of 2, where bar(2^m) = m. From 65536 = 2^16 the chain is 65536, 16, 4, 2, 1, which is five numbers, so foo = 5. From 32 = 2^5 it is 32, 5, 2, 1, only four numbers. From 65535 the first step gives 15, then 3, then 1, again four numbers. So 65536 is where the count first reaches five.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

Which ONE of the following will be the output of the program?

solutionDiagram.alt: The array of 15 cells before and after the call: cells 2 to 13 are copied onto cells 0 to 11 so cells 0 to 11 read Hello World!, while cells 12 and 13 keep their old d and exclamation mark, and the terminator stays at cell 14.

steps.title: Strings, and what the copy loop does
steps.body: A C string is an array of characters followed by a terminator, the character with code 0, written \0. printf with %s prints from the first cell up to, but not including, the first \0. The expression *s++ = *t++ copies the character that t points to into the cell s points to, then moves both pointers one cell right. The loop while(*t) runs until t points at a \0. The rule: the loop writes only the cells that s visits, and no terminator is written, so the string still ends where the old terminator was.

steps.title: Lay out the array
steps.body: char a[30] = "@#Hello World!" fills cells 0 to 13 with @ # H e l l o (space) W o r l d !, and all remaining cells, from 14 on, with \0. The call gives s = a (cell 0) and t = a + 2 (cell 2).

steps.title: Copy 12 characters
steps.body: Pass k copies cell k + 2 into cell k, for k = 0 to 11, and then t points to cell 14, which holds \0, so the loop stops. Since s is behind t by two cells, each cell is read before anything overwrites it. Cells 0 to 11 now read Hello World!. Cells 12 and 13 were never written, so they still hold d and !. Cell 14 is still \0. The string printed is therefore Hello World!d!, which is option D.

shortcut.body: The call slides the text two places to the left and never moves the terminator. The last two old characters, d and !, stay in cells 12 and 13 right in front of the old terminator, so the output is Hello World! followed by d!.

traps.text: Believing that the copy changes nothing because source and destination overlap. The loop does write cells 0 to 11, so the visible string changes.
Treating stringcopy as strcpy, which also copies the terminator and would end the string after the exclamation mark. This loop stops before copying the terminator, so the d! survives.

Two slips at once: skipping the H as well (a + 3 instead of a + 2) and assuming the terminator is copied as in strcpy. Neither alone gives this output, since a three-cell slide still leaves l, d and ! behind and prints ello World!ld!. The offset is a + 2, which skips only @ and #.

recognize.clues: A hand-written copy loop with *s++ = *t++ and a source that starts two cells inside the same array: the string is changed in place and the marker is not copied.
recognize.contrast: The library strcpy also copies the marker, which would end the string at once. This loop does not, so cells past the last copied one keep their old characters.

check.body: Count cells instead of reading the text. The string had 14 characters before the call, and the 12 passes overwrite cells 0 to 11, leaving cells 12 and 13 as they were. The printed length is therefore still 14, which any option shorter than that cannot match.

questions.stem: The output of the given C code segment is ________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Trace of x and y through the do-while loop: (126,105), (21,105), (21,84), (21,63), (21,42), (21,21); the loop stops there and prints 21.

steps.title: The do-while loop and the subtraction rule
steps.body: A do-while loop runs its body once and then repeats it as long as the condition after while is true. Here the body subtracts the smaller of x and y from the larger, and the loop ends when x equals y. Replacing the larger of two positive numbers by the difference keeps every common divisor of the pair, so the greatest common divisor never changes. The rule: when the two numbers become equal, that value is their gcd, and it is what printf shows.

steps.title: Trace the values
steps.body: Start (x, y) = (126, 105). x > y, so x = 126 - 105 = 21: (21, 105). Now y is larger: y = 105 - 21 = 84, then 84 - 21 = 63, then 63 - 21 = 42, then 42 - 21 = 21. The pair is (21, 21), the test x != y is false, and the loop ends. printf prints 21. A compiled run printed the same trace and the result 21.

shortcut.body: This is Euclid's algorithm by subtraction, so the output is gcd(126, 105). 126 - 105 = 21 and 21 divides 105 (105 = 5 x 21), so the answer is 21. The shortcut is unsafe if either number could be 0 or negative, where the loop would never stop.

traps.text: Answering 630, the least common multiple. The subtraction loop finds the greatest common divisor, not the lowest common multiple.
Answering 3: factoring 126 = 2 x 3 x 3 x 7 and 105 = 3 x 5 x 7 and keeping only one common factor. The common factors are 3 and 7, so the gcd is 21.
Answering 231 by adding the numbers, or 105 by reading y's starting value. Both x and y end at 21, and the loop only subtracts.

steps.body: In int arr[5] = {30, 50, 10}, the listed values go to arr[0], arr[1], arr[2] and the remaining cells arr[3] and arr[4] are set to 0. Adding 1 to an int pointer moves it to the next element, so &arr[0] + 1 is &arr[1]. The expression *ptr is the element ptr points to. The rule: (*ptr)++ increases the element's value and leaves ptr alone, whereas ptr++ moves ptr to the next element. And a = *ptr copies a value, so a does not follow later changes to the element.

steps.body: ptr points to arr[1]. a = *ptr gives a = 50. (*ptr)++ makes arr[1] = 51; a stays 50. ptr++ makes ptr point to arr[2], so *ptr = 10. The printf adds a + *ptr + arr[1] = 50 + 10 + 51 = 111. A compiled run printed a = 50, *ptr = 10, arr[1] = 51 and 111.

solutionDiagram.alt: The array 0 1 2 2 2 0 0 1 1 with a plus one under cells 0, 1, 4, 6 and 8, and underlines that group the array into five runs of equal values.

steps.title: Recursion on a shrinking array
steps.body: In C, S + 1 is a pointer to the second element of S, so foo(S+1, size-1) runs the same function on the array without its first element. Each call looks at the first two elements and either adds 1 or adds nothing before it recurses. The base cases are size 0, which returns 0, and size 1, which returns 1. The rule: a call adds 1 exactly when S[0] differs from S[1], and the last element always contributes the base-case 1, so foo counts the runs of equal consecutive values.

steps.title: Walk down the array
steps.body: A = 0 1 2 2 2 0 0 1 1. Compare each element with the next: (0,1) differs, +1. (1,2) differs, +1. (2,2) equal, 0. (2,2) equal, 0. (2,0) differs, +1. (0,0) equal, 0. (0,1) differs, +1. (1,1) equal, 0. Then the last call has size 1 and returns 1. The total is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5, one for each run: 0 | 1 | 2 2 2 | 0 0 | 1 1. A compiled run printed 5.

shortcut.body: Count blocks of equal neighbours: 0 | 1 | 2 2 2 | 0 0 | 1 1, which is 5 blocks. Each block ends in exactly one "+1" step, and the final block ends in the base case.

traps.text: Answering 9: thinking every call adds 1, so the value is the length. A call adds 1 only when the first two elements differ.
Answering 4: counting only the changes and forgetting that size == 1 returns 1 for the last element. There are 4 changes and 5 runs.
Answering 3, the number of distinct values 0, 1, 2. The function counts runs, and the value 0 and the value 1 each form two separate runs.

recognize.clues: A recursive function over S+1 with size-1, two base cases and a comparison S[0] != S[1]: trace the calls and see what is being counted.
recognize.contrast: Counting distinct values would need a set or sorting. This function compares only neighbours, so repeated values far apart are counted again.

check.body: Group the array into maximal blocks of equal neighbours and count the blocks. Each block boundary is one change, and the last block closes at the base case, so the count of blocks and the count of changes plus one must match the traced value.

steps.title: Peeling digits with integer division
steps.body: With integer division, n / t is the leading digit of n when t is the power of ten of the same length as n, and n % t is what remains after removing that digit. The first loop multiplies t by 10 until t is larger than n, and then t /= 10 makes it the largest power of ten not above n: for 14362 that is 10000. The statement newnum = 10 * newnum + d appends the digit d on the right of newnum. The variable turn flips between 0 and 1 and the digit is appended only when turn is 1. The rule: the function keeps every second digit, starting from the second.

steps.body: With t = 10000: d = 1, turn = 0, skipped; turn becomes 1. d = 4 (n = 362), turn = 1, so newnum = 4; turn becomes 0. d = 3, skipped. d = 6, turn = 1, newnum = 10 * 4 + 6 = 46. d = 2, turn = 0, skipped. Then t is 0 and the loop ends. The function returns 46. A compiled run traced the same values.

solutionDiagram.alt: Sequence of events: h(20) prints 20, g(10) prints 10, then f(10, 20) runs and g(x) prints 10 and h(y) prints 20, so the output tape reads 20, 10, 10, 20.

steps.title: Arguments with side effects and the order of evaluation
steps.body: The functions g and h print their argument and return it, so calling them has a side effect: output. In f(g(10), h(20)) the two arguments are themselves calls, and they run before f starts. Standard C does not say in which order the arguments are evaluated, but this question fixes it: right to left. The rule: the digits appear in the order in which the calls actually execute, so list the executions in order.

steps.title: Execute in order
steps.body: Right-to-left means the last argument, h(20), runs first: it prints 20 and returns 20. Then g(10) runs: it prints 10 and returns 10. Now f(10, 20) starts with x = 10 and y = 20. Its body calls g(x), which prints 10, and then h(y), which prints 20. The printed digits are 20, 10, 10, 20: 20101020, option A. A C program that called h(20) before g(10) explicitly printed the same string. The other options come from reading the argument order, the body order, or both, the wrong way round.

shortcut.body: Write the argument calls right to left first: 20 then 10. Then write the body of f in source order: g(x) = 10 then h(y) = 20. Put together: 20 10 10 20.

traps.text: Evaluating the arguments left to right (10 20) and then running the body of f backwards, h before g (20 10). The body runs in source order, g(x) then h(y).
Getting the argument order right (20 10) but running the body of f backwards (20 10). Statements in a function body execute top to bottom: g(x) prints 10 first.
Evaluating left to right and ignoring the stated assumption. Left to right gives 10 20 for the arguments and 10 20 for the body; the question says the opposite order for parameters.

recognize.clues: Arguments that are calls with printf inside them, plus the explicit assumption about the order of evaluation of parameters: output order depends on it.
recognize.contrast: In real C the order of evaluating arguments is unspecified, so without the stated assumption the output could not be fixed. The body of f, by contrast, always runs in source order.

check.body: Test the options against two facts. The first digits come from the argument calls, and the last argument h(20) runs first, so the output must start with 20; that removes 10202010 and 10201020. The last digits come from the body of f, which runs g(x) then h(y), so the output must end with 1020; that removes 20102010. Only 20101020 satisfies both.

Consider the following C function definition.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The function call fX("abcd") will always return a value
Assuming a character array c is declared as char c[] = "abcd" in main(), the function call fX(c) will always return a value
The code of the function will not compile
Assuming a character pointer c is declared as char *c = "abcd" in main(), the function call fX(c) will always return a value

solutionDiagram.alt: The string abcd with its terminator in cells 0 to 4: pointer b starts with a at cell 0 and moves right until it reaches the terminator at cell 4, so b minus a is 4.

steps.title: Strings, char pointers and pointer difference
steps.body: A C string is a run of characters followed by the terminator character \0, and a char * points at one of its characters. The loop while(*b) b++ moves b right until it points at \0, so it measures the length of the string. For two pointers into the same array, b - a is the number of elements between them, here a character count. A string literal such as "abcd" is an array of 5 characters, a, b, c, d and \0, that the program may read but must not modify. The rule: a call returns a value when the loop reaches a terminator, and fX only reads.

steps.title: Judge each statement
steps.body: A: fX("abcd") passes the literal; b walks 4 cells and the call returns 4, true. B: char c[] = "abcd" is a 5-element array with the same contents; the array name becomes a pointer to its first element, and the call returns 4, true. C: the function is valid C (a pointer comparison in the loop, a pointer difference returned as an int), so it compiles; the statement is false. D: char *c = "abcd" points to the literal, and fX reads it only, so it returns 4, true. A compiled run printed 4 for all three calls. The answer is A, B and D.

shortcut.body: fX is strlen written by hand. All three calls pass a properly terminated "abcd" and the function never writes, so each returns 4. The code is valid C, so C is false. Select A, B, D.

traps.text: Selecting C because b - a looks like a pointer subtraction that cannot be returned as an int. Subtracting two pointers into the same array is valid and gives a count, and returning it as an int compiles.
Leaving out D because "a pointer to a string literal is read-only". Only modifying a literal is undefined behaviour. fX reads, so the call is fine.
Leaving out B because an array is not a pointer. An array argument converts to a pointer to its first element, so fX(c) behaves exactly as fX with a literal.

recognize.clues: A while(*b) loop that advances a char pointer and a final b - a: this is a hand-written length scan, and each option passes the same text in a different form.
recognize.contrast: A pointer to a string literal and a char array initialised from the same literal are different objects, but this function only reads, so the difference does not matter here.

check.body: Substitute the concrete string. The text abcd has four characters before its terminator, so the pointer travels four cells in every form passed, which gives the same value each time. A compiler would also accept the function, because every operation in it is valid on char pointers.

solutionDiagram.alt: The array of two doubles of 8 bytes each: p points to a[0] and q to a[1]; the byte gap of 8 is one element, so q minus p is 1, and the values differ by 5.

steps.title: Pointer arithmetic counts elements
steps.body: A pointer of type double * moves in whole doubles: p + 1 points to the next double, which is sizeof(double) = 8 bytes later. Subtracting two pointers into the same array divides the byte gap by the element size, so q - p counts elements, not bytes. Dereferencing, *q, gives the double stored at q. A cast (int) of a double drops the fraction. The rule: pointer difference is a count of elements, and *q - *p is a difference of stored values.

steps.title: Evaluate the two numbers
steps.body: p = a points to a[0] and q = p + 1 points to a[1]. The byte gap is 8, so q - p = 8 / 8 = 1. The values give *q - *p = 25.0 - 20.0 = 5.0, and the cast turns it into 5. printf prints 1,5, which is option B. A compiled run printed 1,5 and a byte gap of 8.

shortcut.body: The pointers sit on adjacent elements, so q - p = 1 with no calculation. The second number is 25 - 20 = 5. Answer 1,5.

traps.text: No single consistent slip produces 4,8, so it is a distractor. The nearest source is recalling type sizes, 4 for int and 8 for double, and printing them instead of computing. The distance between adjacent elements is 1 and the difference of stored values is 5.
Choosing 8,5: reporting the byte gap, 8, for q - p. The subtraction of two pointers is divided by the element size, so the answer is 1 element.
Choosing 1,8: pairing the correct distance with 8, the size of a double, in place of *q - *p. The second expression subtracts the two stored values, 25.0 - 20.0.

recognize.clues: Two double pointers into one array, q = p + 1, and the expression q - p cast to int next to *q - *p: one is about positions, the other about contents.
recognize.contrast: q - p measures distance in elements, while (char *)q - (char *)p would measure bytes. The size of the element type decides the gap between them.

check.body: Rewrite q - p using the definition: the address gap in bytes divided by the element size. Because q was built as p + 1, the gap is exactly one element size, so the quotient is fixed without knowing what sizeof(double) is. The second number needs only the two stored values.

solutionDiagram.alt: Loop cycle of the test a < 10, the update a = a / 12 + 1 and a += b, with a table showing a equal to 6 at the start and 1 after every pass, so the loop never ends.

steps.title: Integer division and when a loop ends
steps.body: When both operands of / are int, C divides and throws the fraction away, so 6 / 12 is 0, not 0.5. A while loop tests its condition before every pass and stops only when the condition is false. The rule: to decide whether a loop ends, follow the variable in the condition and ask whether the body can ever make the condition false.

steps.title: Run the loop
steps.body: Start with a = 6 and b = 0. The test 6 < 10 is true, so the body runs: a = 6 / 12 + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1, then a += 0 leaves a = 1. The test 1 < 10 is true, so the body runs again: 1 / 12 is 0, so a = 1 once more. Every pass gives a = 1, because any a from 0 to 11 satisfies a / 12 = 0. The value a never reaches 10, the test never fails, and printf is never reached. A run with a pass counter confirmed a = 1 on every pass. The program gets stuck in an infinite loop: option C.

shortcut.body: Notice that a / 12 + 1 equals 1 for every a below 12, and b = 0 adds nothing. So a is pinned at 1, which is below 10 forever. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Expecting a to climb step by step and stop just below 10. The update does not add to a; it replaces a by a / 12 + 1, which is 1 each time.
Expecting the loop to end with a = 10, the first value that fails a < 10. The body never produces a value that large.
Printing the starting 6 as if the body did not run. The test 6 < 10 is true, so the body runs, and the loop then never exits to reach printf.

recognize.clues: Two int operands around / in the update a = a / 12 + 1, together with a while test a < 10 that depends only on a.
recognize.contrast: Looks like a counting loop that climbs towards 10, but the body replaces a rather than adding to it, so there is no climb.

check.body: Ask what it would take to escape: the new a is at least 10 only when a / 12 is at least 9, so a must already be 108 or more. Starting from 6 and always returning to 1, a never gets near 108, which agrees with the trace.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

Assume that the input to the program from the command line is 1234 followed by a newline character. Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: The program will terminate with no output
The program will terminate with 4321 as output
The program will terminate with 1234 as output

solutionDiagram.alt: Five nested calls of fX read 1, 2, 3, 4 and newline going down the stack; the print statements run on the way back up in the order 4, 3, 2, 1.

steps.title: Frames and the order of work around a recursive call
steps.body: Each call of a function gets its own frame, a private set of local variables; here every call has its own char a. getchar() reads the next unread character of the input and returns it, so successive calls read successive characters. A statement written after a recursive call runs only when that call returns, so the later calls finish first. The rule: work before the recursive call happens in call order going down; work after it happens in reverse order coming back up.

steps.title: Going down: the reads
steps.body: Call 1 reads '1', which is not newline, so it calls fX. Call 2 reads '2', call 3 reads '3', call 4 reads '4', and each calls fX again. Call 5 reads the newline, so its test fails and it makes no recursive call. Its second if also fails because a is newline, so it prints nothing and returns. The recursion stops, so the program terminates.

steps.title: Coming back: the prints
steps.body: Call 4 resumes after its recursive call with a = '4', which is not newline, so putchar prints 4 and it returns. Call 3 then prints 3, call 2 prints 2 and call 1 prints 1. The characters appear in the order 4, 3, 2, 1. The output is 4321: option C.

shortcut.body: The print comes after the recursive call, so the program reverses the input: 1234 becomes 4321, and the newline itself is not printed. This is unsafe if the putchar sat before the call; then the order would be preserved.

traps.text: Thinking the recursion has no end. It ends when getchar returns the newline, and the input supplies one after 4.
Thinking the newline stops all printing. Only the newline frame skips putchar; the four frames below it each still print their own character.
Reading the output in input order. 1234 would need putchar before the recursive call; here it is after, so the order reverses.

recognize.clues: The only output statement, putchar, sits after the recursive call fX(), and each call reads a fresh character with getchar.
recognize.contrast: A loop or a putchar placed before the call would keep input order; here the placement after the call is what reverses it.

check.body: Try a one-character input such as 7 followed by newline: the first call reads 7, the second reads the newline and returns, then the first prints 7, so a single character is unchanged. Two characters 12 would give 21, which shows the reversal and matches the four-digit trace.

Consider the following C function definition.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the above function?
options: If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$
If the inputs are x=20, y=20, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$
If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is less than $2^{10}$
If the inputs are x=10, y=20, then the return value is greater than $2^{20}$

solutionDiagram.alt: Closed form x after i passes equals 2^i times (x + y) minus y, the ten values of x for f(20,10), and a table comparing f(20,10), f(20,20) and f(10,20) against 2^20 and 2^10.

steps.title: A loop that applies one update y times
steps.body: The loop runs y times (i = 0 to y - 1), and each pass replaces x by x + x + y, that is by 2x + y. Such a rule, where the next value is computed from the previous one, is a recurrence. A standard trick for the form next = 2 * old + y is to add y to both sides: next + y = 2 * old + 2y = 2 * (old + y). So the quantity x + y doubles on every pass.

steps.title: Closed form
steps.body: After y passes the quantity x + y has doubled y times, so x_final + y = 2^y * (x + y). The function therefore returns 2^y * (x + y) - y.

steps.title: Evaluate the three inputs
steps.body: f(20, 10) = 2^10 * 30 - 10 = 30720 - 10 = 30710. With 2^10 = 1024 and 2^20 = 1048576, this is above 2^10 and below 2^20, so statement A is false and statement C is false. f(20, 20) = 2^20 * 40 - 20 = 41943020, which is above 2^20, so B is true. f(10, 20) = 2^20 * 30 - 20 = 31457260, which is above 2^20, so D is true. Both large values are below 2^31 = 2147483648, so the int does not overflow, and a compiled run printed the same values. True statements: B and D.

shortcut.body: The result is about 2^y * (x + y). For y = 20 that is at least 2^20 * 30, far above 2^20, so B and D are true without arithmetic. For y = 10 it is about 30 * 1024 = 30720: above 2^10, below 2^20, so A and C are false. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Believing x = 20, y = 10 reaches 2^20 because the loop doubles x. It doubles only 10 times, so the value is about 30 * 2^10, not 2^20.
Taking 2^y as the whole answer. The doubling applies to x + y = 30, so the value is 30 times larger than 2^10, and it is above 2^10.
Leaving out B because 41943020 looks too big for an int. It is below 2147483647, so there is no overflow and the comparison holds.
Leaving out D because x = 10 is small. The loop count is y = 20, so the value is 30 * 2^20 - 20, which is above 2^20.

recognize.clues: A for loop that repeats x = x + x + y exactly y times, with statements that compare the result with powers of two.
recognize.contrast: Not a plain doubling of x: the added y means x itself is not multiplied by 2^y, but x + y is.

check.body: Run the smallest case by hand: x = 1, y = 1 gives 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, and the closed form 2^1 * (1 + 1) - 1 = 3 agrees. Also y = 0 runs no pass and returns x, matching 2^0 * (x + 0) - 0.

questions.stem: The integer value printed by the ANSI-C program given below is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The static variable x of funcp in the static segment goes 1, 2, 3 across two calls, while the main frame holds x = 2 and y = 3 + 2 = 5, so x + y = 7.

steps.title: Static local variables
steps.body: A local variable declared static is created once, before main starts, and the initialiser = 1 runs only once, at that moment. It keeps its value between calls to the function, because it lives in the static data area and not in the call's stack frame. An ordinary local such as x in main is a different variable, even though it shares the name. The rule: a static initialiser is not run again on later calls.

steps.title: Trace the two calls
steps.body: The static x starts at 1. First call: x++ makes it 2 and the function returns 2, so main's x becomes 2. Second call: x++ makes the static 3 and the function returns 3. The statement y = funcp() + x then computes 3 + 2 = 5, using main's x = 2 assigned by the previous statement.

steps.title: Print
steps.body: The program prints x + y = 2 + 5 = 7. A compiled run printed 7.

shortcut.body: Write the successive returns of funcp: 2, then 3. So x = 2 and y = 3 + 2 = 5, and the sum is 7.

traps.text: 6 comes from treating the initialiser as running on every call, so each call returns 2: x = 2, y = 2 + 2 = 4, sum 6. The initialiser runs once.
5 is y alone, or the sum 2 + 3 of the two return values. The program prints x + y, and y already includes x.

recognize.clues: The keyword static on a local variable with an initialiser, in a function that is called twice and changes the variable.
recognize.contrast: An ordinary local would be recreated as 1 on every call and return 2 each time; the static keeps its value between calls.

check.body: Check against the alternative reading: if the variable were reset on each call, the result would be 2 + 4 = 6. The static one makes the second call return a larger value than the first, so the printed total must exceed 6.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three memory snapshots of x, z[0] and z[1]: at the start 1, 10, 11; after p = &x and *p = 10 the value x is 10; after the += 3 through &z[0] + 1 the value z[1] is 14.

steps.title: Pointers, & and *
steps.body: A pointer is a variable that holds the address of another variable. &v is the address of v, and *p means the variable that p points to, so *p = 10 writes 10 into that variable. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the next element of its type, so &z[0] + 1 is the address of z[1]. The rule: writing through a pointer changes the variable it points to, and reassigning p changes only where p points.

steps.title: Follow the writes
steps.body: p = &x makes p point to x, and *p = 10 writes into x, so x = 10. The line p = &z[1] only moves p; no value changes. Then &z[0] + 1 is &z[1], so *(&z[0] + 1) += 3 adds 3 to z[1]: 11 + 3 = 14. The element z[0] is never written and stays 10.

steps.title: Print
steps.body: x, z[0], z[1] are 10, 10, 14, so the output is 10, 10, 14: option D. A compiled run agreed.

shortcut.body: Only two stores happen: x through p, and z[1] through the address &z[0] + 1. So x = 10, z[1] = 14, and z[0] keeps 10.

traps.text: Believing the writes do not reach the variables. *p = 10 writes into x, and the += 3 writes into z[1].
Forgetting that p pointed to x when *p = 10 ran, so x stays 1. The assignment p = &x came first.
Computing 11 + 3 = 14 correctly but storing it in z[0]. The sum is right because &z[0] + 1 is z[1], which holds 11, so the 14 belongs in z[1] and z[0] stays 10.

recognize.clues: The expression *(&z[0] + 1) += 3 and the pointer p reassigned between x and an array element.
recognize.contrast: The assignment p = &z[1] looks like a store but only retargets p, so no array value changes there.

check.body: Count the stores: exactly two writes reach memory, one into x and one into an array element. So only two of the three printed values can differ from their starting values 1, 10 and 11, which the final values satisfy.

solutionDiagram.alt: Three 3 by 3 blocks holding 1 to 9, 10 to 18 and 19 to 27 with the first row of each block shaded; the loop prints those rows as 1 2 3, 10 11 12 and 19 20 21.

steps.title: Three-dimensional arrays and initialiser braces
steps.body: int a[3][3][3] is 3 blocks, each block being 3 rows of 3 ints. In a[i][j][k], i picks the block, j the row inside the block and k the column. Memory is row-major: the last index changes fastest, so the 27 ints sit in the order a[0][0][0], a[0][0][1], and so on. In an initialiser, a brace group fills one sub-array and values inside it fill in memory order. The rule: each inner group of 9 values fills one whole block, row by row.

steps.title: Fill the array
steps.body: The first group {1, ..., 9} fills a[0]: row 0 is 1 2 3, row 1 is 4 5 6, row 2 is 7 8 9. The second group fills a[1] with 10 11 12 / 13 14 15 / 16 17 18, and the third fills a[2] with 19 20 21 / 22 23 24 / 25 26 27.

steps.title: Read with j fixed at 0
steps.body: The loops change only i and k; j stays 0. So each line is row 0 of block i: a[0][0] = 1 2 3, a[1][0] = 10 11 12 and a[2][0] = 19 20 21. That is option A.

shortcut.body: With j = 0 fixed, every line is the first row of a block. Block i starts at 9i + 1, so the lines are 1 2 3, 10 11 12, 19 20 21. Unsafe only if the braces are grouped differently from 9 per block.

traps.text: Treating k as the row index, which gives a[i][k][0]. In the code k is the last subscript, the column, so consecutive k are adjacent numbers.
Ignoring the block index i and walking the rows of the first block. The loop variable i selects the block, so the numbers jump to 10 and 19.
Reading the row as following i, as in a[i][i][k]. The row index j is fixed at 0, so the second line is 10 11 12, not 13 14 15.

recognize.clues: A three-subscript array a[3][3][3] filled from flat brace groups, read with j held at 0 while i and k loop.
recognize.contrast: Not the same as a[i][i][k]: here the middle index is constant, so each line is the same row position in a different block.

check.body: Cross-check with the flat position 9i + 3j + k. With j = 0 the line for block i starts at flat 9i, which holds the value 9i + 1, giving 1, 10 and 19 as the first numbers of the lines.

questions.stem:
What is printed by the following ANSI C program?

ASCII encoding for relevant characters is given below

solutionDiagram.alt: Bit patterns of P = 1010000 and x = 1111000 with their AND 1010000 = 80, OR 1111000 = 120 and XOR 0101000 = 40, then the constants added and the characters z, K and S printed.

steps.title: Characters are numbers, and the three bit operators
steps.body: A char holds a small integer, its ASCII code, so 'P' is the number 80, and arithmetic on chars is ordinary integer arithmetic. The operators &, | and ^ work on the binary digits of two numbers, one position at a time: & gives 1 only where both digits are 1, | gives 1 where at least one digit is 1, and ^ gives 1 where the digits differ. printf with %c prints the character whose code is the value, while %d would print the number. The rule: convert to numbers, apply the bit operator, add or subtract, and convert back.

steps.title: Codes and binary
steps.body: 'P' is the 16th capital letter, so its code is 65 + 15 = 80 = 1010000 in binary. 'x' is the 24th small letter, so its code is 97 + 23 = 120 = 1111000.

steps.title: The three expressions
steps.body: AND: 1010000 = 80, then 80 + 42 = 122, which is 'z'. OR: 1111000 = 120, then 120 - 45 = 75, which is 'K' (65 + 10). XOR: 0101000 = 40, then 40 + 43 = 83, which is 'S' (65 + 18). The call prints the characters z K S: option A.

shortcut.body: 80 is 64 + 16 and 120 is 64 + 32 + 16 + 8. The AND keeps the shared 64 + 16 = 80, the OR keeps all four = 120, the XOR keeps what differs, 32 + 8 = 40. Add 42, subtract 45, add 43, and read the codes as letters. Option B is out at once because %c prints characters, not numbers.

traps.text: Reading the format as %d. The format is %c, so the codes 122, 75 and 83 print as the characters z, K and S.
Seeing only the three constants '*', '-' and '+', as if each bit operation gave 0. The operations combine the codes of P and x and give 80, 120 and 40.
Expecting the operators to hand back a and b. They combine two codes into a new code, and the constants are then added or subtracted.

recognize.clues: The operators &, | and ^ applied to two char variables, with an ASCII table supplied and the result printed with %c.
recognize.contrast: Not logical && or ||: these operators work on every bit position and give a number, not just 0 or 1.

check.body: For two numbers a and b, a & b plus a | b equals a + b. Here 80 + 120 = 200 and the AND and OR codes sum to 200, and a ^ b equals (a | b) minus (a & b), which checks each pair of codes independently.

solutionDiagram.alt: A 4 by 5 grid with arr[i][j] = 10*i + j and flat positions 0 to 19; arr[1] starts at flat 5 with value 10, adding 9 reaches flat 14, which is row 2 column 4 with value 24.

steps.title: Row-major layout and pointer steps
steps.body: A two-dimensional array arr[4][5] is stored as 20 ints in one block, row after row (row-major), so arr[i][j] sits at flat position 5i + j. In an expression, arr[1] (a row) turns into a pointer to its first int. Adding n to an int pointer moves it n ints on, and nothing marks the end of a row. The rule: pointer arithmetic walks the flat memory, so it runs across row boundaries.

steps.title: Locate the element
steps.body: The loops store 10*i + j at arr[i][j]. arr[1] points to flat position 5. Adding 9 gives flat position 14. Flat 14 is row 14 / 5 = 2 and column 14 mod 5 = 4, so the pointer lands on arr[2][4].

steps.title: Read the value
steps.body: *(arr[1] + 9) is arr[2][4] = 10*2 + 4 = 24: option C. A compiled run printed 24.

shortcut.body: Offset 9 from the start of row 1 is one full row (5) plus 4 more. So the element is arr[2][4], whose value 10*2 + 4 = 24 is read off the formula.

traps.text: Reading the expression as arr[1][4], stopping at the end of row 1. The offset 9 is larger than the row length and carries on into row 2.
Moving by one row (5 ints) instead of 9 ints: that lands on flat 10, arr[2][0] = 20.
Being one step too far, as if the offset were 10: flat 15 is arr[3][0] = 30. Offset 9 stops at flat 14.

recognize.clues: The expression *(arr[1] + 9) uses an offset larger than the row length of 5, applied to a row of a 2D array.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI C function:

The value returned by SomeFunction(15, 255) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain of calls (15,255), (15,240), (15,225), down to (15,45), (15,30), (15,15); at each step y loses 15, and the last call returns 15.

steps.title: What the function does
steps.body: The function replaces the larger argument by the difference of the two until the arguments are equal. That is the subtractive form of Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (gcd): any number that divides both x and y also divides x - y, so gcd(x, y) = gcd(x - y, y), and when the two arguments are equal their common value is the gcd. The rule: the calls change x and y while the gcd stays the same, until x = y. The first test returns 1 only if an argument becomes exactly 1.

steps.title: Trace the calls
steps.body: Start with (15, 255). Here y is larger, so the call is (15, 240), then (15, 225), and so on, with y losing 15 each time. Since 255 = 17 * 15, the values of y are multiples of 15 and the sequence ends at (15, 15) after 16 steps. No argument is ever 1 on the way, since x stays 15 and y stays a multiple of 15.

steps.title: Return
steps.body: At (15, 15) the test x == y is true, so the function returns x = 15. The same value comes back through every earlier call, so SomeFunction(15, 255) = 15 = gcd(15, 255).

shortcut.body: Recognise subtractive Euclid: the result is gcd(15, 255). Since 15 divides 255, the gcd is 15. This holds because no argument reaches 1 on the way; when the gcd is 1, the first base case gives 1 too.

traps.text: 1: assuming the first base case fires. Neither argument ever equals 1, because every y is a multiple of 15.
17: the quotient 255 / 15, the number of subtractions plus one, instead of the value returned. The function returns the common value 15.
255 or 240: returning the larger argument from an early call. Only the final equal pair returns a value, and it is 15.

recognize.clues: Two arguments, one test for equality, and each branch calls the function with the larger argument reduced by the smaller one; the first base case can only fire at exactly 1.
recognize.contrast: It resembles a plain countdown recursion, but both arguments take part: the value that is returned is the common value where they meet, not a count of the calls.

check.body: Divide the original pair by the returned value: 15 / 15 = 1 and 255 / 15 = 17, both whole numbers, and 1 and 17 share no factor above 1. So the returned value divides both arguments and cannot be made larger, which is what the subtractive method must give.

Consider the following ANSI C program:

Which one of the statements below is correct about the program?
options: Upon execution, the program creates a linked-list of five nodes.
Upon execution, the program goes into an infinite loop.
It has a missing return which will be reported as an error by the compiler.
It dereferences an uninitialized pointer that may result in a run-time error.

solutionDiagram.alt: A linked list of four nodes holding 0, 1, 2 and 3; the next pointer of the last node is never set, and the second loop dereferences it at index 3.

steps.title: Linked lists and uninitialised memory
steps.body: A linked list is a chain of nodes; each struct Node holds a value and a next pointer to the following node, and the last node's next should be NULL. malloc returns a block of memory whose contents are not set, so a field holds garbage until the program assigns it. Reading through a pointer that holds garbage (head->value) is undefined behaviour and usually crashes. The rule: count which next pointers are assigned and see whether the walk goes beyond them.

steps.title: What the first part builds
steps.body: The first malloc creates the head node with value 0; its next is not yet set. The loop runs for index 1, 2 and 3. Each pass allocates a node, links the previous end to it, stores the index and moves boxE forward. The list is therefore head(0) -> 1 -> 2 -> 3: four nodes, not five, so option A is false. The next pointers of nodes 0, 1 and 2 are set, but node 3's next is never assigned and holds garbage.

steps.title: The walk
steps.body: The second loop has a fixed bound, index 0 to 3, so it cannot be infinite (option B is false). In each pass it prints head->value, moves head one node on, and prints head->value again. At index 0 it prints 0 and 1, at index 1 it prints 1 and 2, at index 2 it prints 2 and 3. At index 3 it prints 3, then head = head->next copies node 3's uninitialised next, and head->value dereferences it. That is option D. Option C is false because a missing return in main is accepted: the compiler does not report an error.

shortcut.body: Count nodes: one head plus three from the loop is four, which rules out A. The last pass of the walk needs a fourth next pointer, and the program never set one, so D. B fails because the loop is bounded; C fails because main need not return. About a minute.

traps.text: Counting the indexes 0 to 3 and then adding the head, which gives five. The head is the node with value 0, so there are four nodes.
Expecting the list to circle round forever. The loop is a for loop with a fixed bound; the real fault is the garbage pointer at its last pass.
Believing main must end with return. In C, falling off the end of main is legal and returns 0 (C99 and later), so no compiler error is reported.

recognize.clues: A struct with a next pointer, nodes obtained with malloc, and a second loop that moves head forward once per pass with a bound written separately from the first loop.
recognize.contrast: It looks like a question about list length or an infinite loop, but the walk is bounded; what decides it is whether every pointer the walk follows was actually assigned.

check.body: Make the walk safe and see what changes: if the second loop ran only for index 0 to 2, it would follow just three next pointers, all of which were set, and no fault would arise. The extra pass at index 3 is exactly the one that touches the unset pointer, which confirms where the problem lies.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI C program.

The output of the program upon execution is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: A 3 by 3 grid of pending calls, x reduced by 10 across and y reduced by 10 down, with path counts 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 / 1 3 6; the bottom-right call, where both x and y are at most 0, is reached by 6 paths and each returns 10, giving 60.

steps.title: A recursion that adds up its leaves
steps.body: A call with x > 0 and y > 0 makes two calls and returns the sum of their results. A call with only one argument still positive makes one call and passes its result up. A call with both arguments at most 0 returns q and calls nothing: this is a leaf. So the value of the top call is the sum of the values returned by all leaves, and every leaf returns q. The rule: result = q * (number of distinct call paths that end in a leaf).

steps.title: Count the call paths
steps.body: Here q = 10. Each x-call lowers x by 10, so x goes 15, 5, -5: two such steps make x at most 0. y behaves the same way. Describe a call by the pair (a, b), where a is the number of x-steps taken and b the number of y-steps. From (0, 0) the function may take an x-step or a y-step, until a = 2 or b = 2; after that only the other kind of step is possible and nothing branches. A leaf is the state (2, 2). The number of paths to it is the number of orderings of 2 x-steps and 2 y-steps. Filling each cell with the sum of the cell above and the cell to its left, starting from 1 along the border, gives 1 1 1 / 1 2 3 / 1 3 6, so there are 6 paths.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Six leaves, each returning q = 10, give 6 * 10 = 60. A compiled run printed 60.

shortcut.body: The number of steps per axis is the smallest k with 15 - 10k <= 0, which is k = 2. The paths to the leaf number C(4, 2) = 6, and each returns 10: 60. Unsafe if the steps per axis differ, but the border cells still give 1 path, so the grid method works for any sizes.

traps.text: 10: following one branch only and returning q once. The top call adds the results of two calls at every call with both arguments positive.
20: stopping after one subtraction per axis. After x = 15 - 10 = 5, x is still positive, so another step is needed and the leaf is two steps away.
200: taking three steps per axis, which counts 20 paths. x = 5 - 10 = -5 is already at most 0, so two steps are enough.

recognize.clues: Two recursive calls that are added, one argument reduced by q in each, and base cases that depend on x and y being at most 0 and return the constant q.
recognize.contrast: Naive branching suggests an exponential count of calls, but because only two kinds of step exist, the leaves can be counted as lattice paths instead of by writing out the whole tree.

check.body: Count a smaller case by hand with the same method: for foo(5, 5, 10) both arguments reach 0 or below after one step, so the two calls foo(5, -5, 10) and foo(-5, 5, 10) each go on to one leaf. That gives 2 paths, the binomial coefficient for one step of each kind, and the grid rule agrees with the direct count.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI C program.

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: The program will not compile successfully.
The program will compile successfully and output 10 when executed.
The program will compile successfully and output 8 when executed.
The program will compile successfully and output 13 when executed.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table over j from -3 to 3 showing whether i++ runs, the value of i++, the value of i, and count; i++ is skipped for j below 0, then count adds 1, 2 and 3 for j = 1, 2, 3, ending with count 6 and i 4.

steps.title: Short-circuit && and post-increment
steps.body: The operator && evaluates its left operand first. If that is false (0), the result is false and the right operand is not evaluated at all (short-circuit). If the left is true, the right is evaluated. The expression i++ is a post-increment: its value is the old value of i, and i then increases by 1. In a condition, 0 is false and any other value is true. The rule: the right side of && runs only when the left side is true, and i++ yields the value before the increment.

steps.title: Run the loop
steps.body: For j = -3, -2, -1 the left side j >= 0 is false, so i++ is skipped: i stays 0 and count stays 0. For j = 0 the left side is true, so i++ runs: it yields the old value 0 (false) and i becomes 1, so the body is skipped. For j = 1, i++ yields 1 (true), so count = 0 + 1 = 1 and i = 2. For j = 2 it yields 2, count = 1 + 2 = 3, i = 3. For j = 3 it yields 3, count = 3 + 3 = 6, i = 4.

steps.title: After the loop
steps.body: The program compiles without trouble, since an int is a valid condition. count = count + i = 6 + 4 = 10, and 10 is printed: option B.

shortcut.body: i++ runs only for j = 0, 1, 2, 3, so i ends at 4. The body runs when the old i is nonzero: j = 1, 2, 3, adding 6. The total is 6 + 4 = 10.

traps.text: Thinking an int cannot be used as a condition. In C any nonzero value is true, so the program compiles.
Ending with i = 2 or counting fewer increments. The increment runs for each of the four values j = 0 to 3, so i ends at 4 and the output is 6 + 4.
Forgetting the short-circuit and running i++ for all seven values of j: i ends at 7 and 6 + 7 = 13. For negative j the right operand is never evaluated.

recognize.clues: A condition of the form (j >= 0) && (i++) inside a loop: a side effect sits on the right of && and its execution depends on the left side.
recognize.contrast: With a bitwise & or an ordinary function call both sides always run, so i would grow on every pass. Only the logical && skips its right operand, and that is what separates the outputs.

check.body: Check the final value of i independently: the right operand is reached only when j >= 0, which holds for four values of j, so i must end at 4. The body adds j only when the old value of i is nonzero, which excludes the first of those four values, so count is the sum of the other three. Combining the two gives the printed value.

questions.stem:
Consider the following ANSI C function:

Let Z be an array of 10 elements with $Z[i]=1$, for all $i$ such that $0 \le i \le 9$. The value returned by SimpleFunction(Z, 10, 2) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The value of total after each of the 9 passes of the loop: 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, 511, 1023, each the double of the previous plus 1.

steps.title: The loop is a repeated update
steps.body: An array parameter Y[] is passed as a pointer to the first element, so Y[k] reads the k-th element of Z. Here n = 10, x = 2 and every Y[k] = 1. The loop runs for loopIndex = 1 up to n - 1 = 9, which is 9 passes, and each pass sets total to x * total + Y[loopIndex] = 2 * total + 1. The rule: apply the update once per pass, and count the passes from the loop bounds.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: total starts at Y[0] = 1. After the nine passes it is 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, 511 and 1023.

steps.title: Why the pattern holds
steps.body: Add 1 to both sides of the update: total + 1 becomes 2 * (total + 1), so total + 1 doubles each pass. It starts at 2 and doubles 9 times, reaching 2^10 = 1024, so total = 1023. In other words total is the binary number with ten 1s.

shortcut.body: Spot that total + 1 doubles: 2, 4, 8, and after 9 passes it is 2^10 = 1024. So the answer is 1023, with no trace needed.

traps.text: 511: running only 8 passes, as if the bound were n - 2. The loop condition is loopIndex <= n - 1, so index 9 is included.
2047: running ten passes, as if the loop started at index 0 or ended at n. The loop starts at 1, since Y[0] is already in total.
1024: reading total + 1 = 2^10 as the return value. The function returns total, which is one less.
512: dropping the + 1 in each pass, so total only doubles: 1 * 2^9. The + 1 each pass is what makes it 1023.

recognize.clues: A for loop that starts at index 1 because Y[0] is already in total, an update of the form x * total + Y[i], and an array whose elements are all equal.
recognize.contrast: The update looks like evaluating a polynomial by Horner's rule, which it is; the equal coefficients make it a geometric sum, so a closed form is quicker than a trace.

check.body: Test the smallest case, n = 2: one pass gives total = 2 * 1 + 1 = 3 = 2^2 - 1, and n = 3 gives 2 * 3 + 1 = 7 = 2^3 - 1. So n elements give 2^n - 1, and n = 10 gives 1023. A second reading: each pass is a left shift by one bit plus a new low bit 1, so ten rounds of it leave a binary number of ten 1s.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program.

The output of the program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The 4 by 5 array holding 1 to 20; **a is 1, so a + **a + 2 is a + 3, the row 16 17 18 19 20, and moving 3 ints along that row reaches 19.

steps.title: Pointer to a row, and the meaning of *(*(a+i)+j)
steps.body: In an expression, the array a (4 rows of 5 ints) becomes a pointer to its first row. Adding n to a row pointer skips n whole rows, and * on a row pointer gives that row, which in turn behaves as a pointer to its first int. Adding m to that int pointer skips m ints, and * reads the int. So *(*(a + i) + j) is exactly a[i][j]. The rule: adding to a row pointer moves by rows, adding to an int pointer moves by ints.

steps.title: Evaluate the inner pieces
steps.body: *a is row 0, a pointer to the int 1, so **a = a[0][0] = 1. Then a + **a + 2 = a + 1 + 2 = a + 3, a pointer to row 3, which is 16 17 18 19 20.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: *(a + 3) is row 3 as a pointer to 16, and adding 3 moves to column 3, the int 19. The expression is a[3][3] = 19, and a compiled run printed 19.

shortcut.body: Rewrite the expression as a[**a + 2][3]. Since **a = 1, that is a[3][3], the fourth entry of the last row: 19.

traps.text: 14: dropping **a and reading a[2][3]. The term **a is the value 1 and it counts as a row offset.
9: taking a + **a as the whole row offset and forgetting the + 2, which gives a[1][3].
16: stopping after *(a + 3), the start of row 3, without moving 3 columns.

recognize.clues: Nested dereferences of a two-dimensional array name, with the stars and the additions mixed in one expression: **a, *(a + ...) and a final + 3 inside.
recognize.contrast: The expression is not a flat walk through memory: a + k moves by whole rows, but the second addition moves by single ints within the chosen row.

check.body: Check by position in row-major order. Row 3 starts after 3 rows of 5 ints, so the element at column 3 is the one with offset 3 * 5 + 3 = 18 from the start, counting from zero. The array holds 1 to 20 in order, so the value at offset 18 is 19.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C functions.

The return value of fun2(5) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the five calls fun2(5) down to fun2(1): fun1 returns 5, 9, 12, 14 and 15, and the static i of fun2 grows 5, 14, 26, 40 and 55.

steps.title: Two different static variables
steps.body: A static local variable is created once and keeps its value across calls, including every level of a recursion. The i inside fun1 and the i inside fun2 share a name but are two separate variables, each belonging to its own function. All calls of fun1 share one i, and all calls of fun2 share another. The rule: a static is never reset, and each function has its own.

steps.title: What fun1 does
steps.body: fun1(n) adds 1 to its i at every level of the recursion, n levels in all (n, n-1, ..., 1), and then returns i. So each call of fun1(n) raises its i by n and returns the new total. Called with 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in turn, fun1 returns 5, 9, 12, 14 and 15.

steps.title: What fun2 does
steps.body: fun2(5) executes i = i + fun1(5) = 0 + 5 = 5, then calls fun2(4): i = 5 + 9 = 14. Then fun2(3) gives 14 + 12 = 26, fun2(2) gives 26 + 14 = 40, and fun2(1) gives 40 + 15 = 55. fun2(0) does nothing and returns i. Every call returns its i only after the deeper calls are done, so each returns the final 55, and fun2(5) returns 55.

shortcut.body: The values of fun1 are the running sums 5, 9, 12, 14, 15, and fun2 adds them all: 5 + 9 + 12 + 14 + 15 = 55.

traps.text: 15: treating fun1's i as an ordinary local that restarts at 0, so fun1(n) returns n: the sum is 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15. The static keeps growing.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C functions.

The value returned by pp(3,4) is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Trace of pp(3, 4): the bits of 4 stored least significant first are 0, 0, 1; ex goes 3, 9, 81, and tot stays 1 until the bit that is 1, where it becomes 81.

steps.title: Binary digits and repeated squaring
steps.body: tob stores the binary digits of b in arr, lowest digit first: b % 2 is the lowest digit and b / 2 drops it. It returns how many digits it stored. pp then keeps ex equal to a, a^2, a^4, a^8, ..., squaring it each pass, so at pass i the value of ex is a^(2^i). When the digit i of b is 1, pp multiplies tot by that ex. Since b is the sum of the powers 2^i whose digits are 1, tot ends as the product of the matching a^(2^i), which is a^b. The rule: digits of the exponent select which squares are multiplied in.

steps.title: Digits of 4
steps.body: tob(4, arr): 4 % 2 = 0, so arr[0] = 0 and b = 2; 2 % 2 = 0, so arr[1] = 0 and b = 1; 1 % 2 = 1, so arr[2] = 1 and b = 0. The function returns 3, and arr = [0, 0, 1].

steps.title: The loop of pp
steps.body: Start with tot = 1 and ex = 3. Pass 0: the digit is 0, so tot stays 1 and ex becomes 9. Pass 1: the digit is 0, so tot stays 1 and ex becomes 81. Pass 2: the digit is 1, so tot = 1 * 81 = 81, and ex is squared again but never used. The function returns 81, which is 3^4.

shortcut.body: pp(a, b) computes a^b by squaring, so pp(3, 4) = 3^4 = 81. This holds while the result fits in an int and b is positive; for b = 0 the loop does not run and tot = 1 = a^0.

traps.text: 12: reading pp as the product a * b. It multiplies powers of a; it never adds or multiplies a by b.
64: swapping the arguments, which gives 4^3. The base is a = 3 and the exponent is b = 4.
6561: returning the final ex instead of tot, or running one pass too many. ex after the last pass is 3^8, but the function returns tot.

recognize.clues: A helper that fills an array using b % 2 and b / 2, followed by a loop that squares one variable every pass and multiplies another only when the stored digit is 1.
recognize.contrast: It resembles an ordinary multiplication loop, but the work is done by squaring and picking by binary digits, so the loop runs about log b times and not b times.

check.body: Check the run against the digit weights. The digits of the exponent from lowest to highest are 0, 0, 1, so only the weight 2^2 is selected. So tot = 3^(2^2) = 3^4 = 81, and multiplying out 3 * 3 * 3 * 3 directly also gives 81. A boundary case agrees: b = 1 has the single digit 1, so tot = a.

Consider the following C program:

The value printed by the program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two panels. Call 1, jumble(5,2): main has x=2, y=5, the parameters are copies 5 and 2, 2*5+2=12 returns and main sets y=12. Call 2, jumble(12,2): 2*12+2=26 returns and main sets x=26, which is printed.

steps.title: Call by value: a parameter is a copy
steps.body: When C calls a function, each parameter is a brand-new variable that starts as a copy of the argument value. Assigning to the parameter inside the function changes only that copy, never the variable in the caller, even if both have the same name. The only thing that travels back is the return value, and it is lost unless the caller stores it. So jumble's x and y are not main's x and y.

steps.title: First call: y = jumble(y, x)
steps.body: The arguments are y = 5 and x = 2, so the parameters are x = 5 and y = 2. Inside, x = 2*5 + 2 = 12 and 12 is returned. main stores it in y, so y = 12. main's x is untouched and is still 2.

steps.title: Second call: x = jumble(y, x)
steps.body: Now y = 12 and x = 2, so the parameters are x = 12 and y = 2. Inside, x = 2*12 + 2 = 26 and 26 is returned. main stores it in its own x, so x = 26. printf prints 26.

shortcut.body: Let f(a, b) = 2a + b. Then y = f(5, 2) = 12 and x = f(12, 2) = 26. Two substitutions, about half a minute.

traps.text: 12: stopping after the first call, or using the old y = 5 again in the second call. The assignment y = jumble(y, x) changes y, so the second call receives 12.

20: writing the first call as jumble(x, y). That gives y = 2*2 + 5 = 9, and the correct second call then gives 2*9 + 2 = 20. The first parameter is the one that gets doubled, and the call passes y first, then x.

recognize.clues: Parameters named x and y inside jumble, the same names as the locals of main, and calls whose arguments are swapped in order: the question tests which copy changes.
recognize.contrast: With pointer parameters the callee could change main's variables. Here the parameters are plain ints, so only the return value carries information back.

check.body: Replay the program with distinct names: u = f(5, 2) gives u = 12, then v = f(12, 2) gives v = 26. The printed value must exceed 2*12 = 24 because the second call adds 2 to a doubled 12.

solutionDiagram.alt: The 13 elements of arr with indices 0 to 12. ip = arr + 4 points at index 4 (value 5); ip[1] is the element at index 5, the value 6, which is printed.

steps.title: Array names, pointer sums and indexing
steps.body: In an expression, the array name arr stands for the address of its first element, arr[0]. Adding k to a pointer moves it k elements forward (the compiler scales by the element size), and p[k] is defined to mean *(p + k), the element k places after p. Indexing starts at 0, so arr[0] is the first value, arr[4] the fifth.

steps.title: Where ip points
steps.body: ip = arr + 4 holds the address of arr[4]. The array is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0, 1, 2, 5, so arr[0..4] = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and *ip is 5.

steps.title: Evaluate ip[1]
steps.body: ip[1] = *(ip + 1) = arr[4 + 1] = arr[5]. Counting from index 0, arr[5] is the sixth value, 6. The program prints 6.

shortcut.body: ip[1] is arr[4 + 1] = arr[5]. Count six values from the start: 1 2 3 4 5 6. The answer is 6.

traps.text: 5: printing *ip (the same as ip[0]), or reading arr[5] as the fifth element. Index 5 is the sixth value because counting starts at 0.
7: moving one place too far, treating ip as arr[5] already and then adding the 1 from ip[1] on top of it.

recognize.clues: A pointer initialised as arr+4 and then used with the subscript form ip[1]: the subscript is applied to the pointer, not to the array name.
recognize.contrast: arr[1] would count from the array start. ip[1] counts from where ip points, so the two give different elements.

check.body: Count positions another way: ip itself is the fifth value in the list, so ip[1] must be the value right after the fifth one. Reading the list left to right after its fifth entry gives the same element as arr[5].
