questions.stem:
Consider the following C function.

Which one of the following will happen when the function convert is called with any positive integer n as argument?
options: It will print the binary representation of n and terminate
It will print the binary representation of n in the reverse order and terminate
It will print the binary representation of n but will not terminate
It will not print anything and will not terminate

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain of calls convert(6), convert(3), convert(1), convert(0), convert(0) and so on. n/2 gives 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, never negative, so the base case n < 0 is not reached, nothing is printed and the recursion does not end.

steps.title: A recursive call waits for the inner call
steps.body: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. Every call has its own n, and the lines after the recursive call run only after that inner call has returned. A call returns only when some call in the chain takes a branch without recursing, the base case. If the chain of arguments never reaches the base case, no call ever returns, so every line after a recursive call never runs. The rule: look at the base case first, then ask whether the arguments can ever satisfy it.

steps.title: Can the base case n < 0 ever be true?
steps.body: The base case here is n < 0, and it is the only branch that prints without recursing. The recursive call passes n/2, and C integer division rounds toward zero. Starting from 6 the arguments are 6, 3, 1, 0, 0, 0, ... Once n is 0, n/2 is 0 again. A non-negative number halved stays non-negative, so no argument is ever negative and the base case is never reached.

steps.title: What the program does
steps.body: No call returns, so printf("%d", n%2) after convert(n/2) never runs, and the base-case printf never runs either. Frames pile up on the stack until it overflows. Nothing is printed and the function does not terminate normally. This is option D. A and B describe a function that returns and prints bits, which would need the usual base case n == 0 or n < 1. C claims bits are printed, but no printf is ever reached because the base case n < 0 never fires.

shortcut.body: Check the base case first: n < 0 can never happen while the argument is n/2 starting from a positive n. The recursion never ends and nothing is printed: D. Safe for any positive n; the order of the printfs does not matter.

traps.text: (A) would be right if the base case were n == 0 and the second printf ran after the inner calls return, which is the textbook binary printer. Here the base case is n < 0, which is never reached.
(B) printing in reverse order needs the printf before the recursive call. The printf here is after it, and anyway no printf is reached.
(C) assumes printing happens while the recursion goes down. The only printf that runs on the way down is the base case n < 0, so nothing is printed.

recognize.clues: The base case is n<0 while the recursive call passes n/2 with integer division, and the question asks what happens for any positive n: check the base case before the printing order.
recognize.contrast: The familiar binary-printing routine stops at n==0 or n<1. Here the test looks like it ends the recursion but a halved non-negative number never turns negative.

check.body: Run n = 1 by hand: the call convert(1) calls convert(0), which calls convert(0) again with the same argument. The argument repeats, so the state repeats and the chain cannot end. Any larger n reaches 1 or 0 on the way down and then gets stuck the same way.

Consider the following C program:

Which one of the following values will be displayed on execution of the programs?

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the eight calls to r(): init returns 7, test 6, body 5 printed, update 4, test 3, body 2 printed, update 1, test 0 which ends the loop. The output is 52.

steps.title: A static local variable and the postfix decrement
steps.body: A static local variable is created once and keeps its value between calls, so num is 7 at the first call, and each call leaves it lower for the next. In return num--, the postfix form hands back the old value and then decreases num. The for loop for (init; test; update) body runs init once, then repeats test, body, update while the test is nonzero. In C, zero is false and anything else is true. The rule: every written r() is a separate call that changes num.

steps.title: Walk the calls in order
steps.body: Init r(): returns 7, num becomes 6. Test r(): returns 6 (true), num 5. Body printf(r()): returns 5, num 4, prints 5. Update r(): returns 4, num 3. Test r(): 3 (true), num 2. Body: returns 2, num 1, prints 2. Update r(): returns 1, num 0. Test r(): returns 0, which is false, num becomes -1, and the loop ends.

steps.title: Read off the output
steps.body: The body ran twice and printed 5 then 2, so the output is 52, option B.

shortcut.body: Each pass uses three calls (test, body, update) and prints the middle one. After init takes 7, the passes take (6, 5, 4) and (3, 2, 1), printing 5 and 2. The next test sees 0 and stops. Answer 52.

traps.text: (A) 41: printing the update call (4 and 1) instead of the call inside printf. The update result is thrown away; the body's r() is the one printed.
(C) 63: printing the value the test returns (6 and 3). The test's r() is a separate call that uses up a value and is not printed.
(D) 630: printing the values the three test calls return (6, 3, then the final 0). It is the same slip as option C carried on to the failing test, which returns 0 and ends the loop before any print.

recognize.clues: A static int inside r() used as the loop test, body and update of a for statement: the hidden state in num is shared across every call.
recognize.contrast: An ordinary local would be reset to 7 at each call and the loop would never end. Static storage is what makes the sequence count down.

check.body: The calls consume the values 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 in order, one per call. The first is init, then triples of test, body, update each take three values, and only the body is printed. The test that sees 0 is the eighth call, which matches a final stop after two passes.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

The number of times the variable sum will be printed, when the above program is executed, is _________________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of the passes: j at the test 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 give i/j of 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 (all above 0.0625) and sum 1.0, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, 1.9375 printed; at j = 32 the value is exactly 0.0625 and the loop ends.

steps.title: How a while loop and float division behave
steps.body: A while loop tests its condition first, and if it is true runs the whole body, then tests again. Here the printf is in the body, so the number of prints equals the number of times the body runs. A float stores numbers of the form m/2^k exactly when m is small, so every value in this program (powers of two and their reciprocals) is stored without rounding error, and comparisons are exact.

steps.title: Turn the condition into a test on j
steps.body: i stays 2.0 and j starts at 1.0. The test i/j > 0.0625 means 2/j > 1/16, that is j < 32. j doubles inside the body, so the values of j at the test are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...

steps.title: Trace the passes
steps.body: j = 1: 2 > 0.0625, body runs, j = 2, sum = 1.0, print. j = 2: 1 > 0.0625, j = 4, sum = 1.5, print. j = 4: 0.5, j = 8, sum = 1.75, print. j = 8: 0.25, j = 16, sum = 1.875, print. j = 16: 0.125, j = 32, sum = 1.9375, print. j = 32: 2/32 = 0.0625, which is not greater than 0.0625, so the loop stops. sum was printed 5 times.

shortcut.body: Rewrite the test as j < 32 and list j = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16: five values. Unsafe if the numbers were not exact binary fractions; here they all are, so the equality case at j = 32 really is equal.

traps.text: 6: letting the pass with j = 32 run. At j = 32 the value of i/j is exactly 0.0625 and the test is strictly greater than, so it fails.
4: counting j after doubling (2, 4, 8, 16) and dropping the first pass. The test uses j before the body doubles it, so j = 1 passes too.

recognize.clues: A while loop whose test depends on a variable that doubles inside the body, with a printf in the body: count how many values of j satisfy the test.
recognize.contrast: A do-while would run the body once before testing. Here the test comes first, and the final value that fails the test with equality matters.

check.body: Check the boundary directly: when j reaches 32 the test compares 2/32 = 0.0625 against 0.0625, which is not strictly greater, so the loop stops there. One step earlier, j = 16 gives 0.125 > 0.0625, so that pass was counted. The passes are exactly j = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

The output of the above C program is __________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The array 2 4 6 8 10 with b pointing at the last element, and a table of i, *b - i, *(b - i) and the term for i = 0 to 4: terms 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, sum 10.

steps.title: A pointer, the value it points to, and who binds first
steps.body: b is a pointer to int. *b is the int stored where b points. b - i is a pointer i elements earlier, and *(b - i) is the int stored there. The expression *b - i is different: the unary * binds tighter than binary -, so it is (*b) - i, an ordinary integer subtraction of i from the value. Pointer arithmetic needs the parentheses around b - i. The rule: * applies first to what directly follows it.

steps.title: Set up the array
steps.body: b = a + 4 points at a[4] = 10. The array holds a[k] = 2(k + 1): 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. So *b = 10 and *(b - i) = a[4 - i] = 10 - 2i.

steps.title: Add up
steps.body: sum = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, and that is printed.

shortcut.body: Each term simplifies to i because a[4 - i] = 10 - 2i, so the sum is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Unsafe only if you misread *b - i as a pointer expression.

traps.text: 0: reading *b - i as *(b - i), the element i places back. Then each term is that element minus itself, 0. The parentheses are on the second part only.
20: dropping the - i from the first part and computing 10 - a[4 - i] = 2i, which sums to 0 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20.

recognize.clues: The mix of *b - i and *(b - i) in one expression, with b set to a+4: one subtracts from a value, the other moves the pointer.
recognize.contrast: *(b - i) and *b - i look nearly identical but differ in precedence: the first dereferences a shifted pointer, the second shifts a dereferenced value.

check.body: Test the loop at its ends by hand. At i = 0 the term is 10 - 10 = 0. At i = 4 it is (10 - 4) - *a = 6 - 2 = 4. The terms rise by 1 each step from 0 to 4, matching a sum of the first five whole numbers.

b - i points i elements before b, so *(b - i) is the array element at position 4 - i here.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program.

The output of this program is:

solutionDiagram.alt: The three bytes of struct p: offset 0 holds the character 1, offset 1 holds 0, offset 2 holds c (97 + 2 = 99). (char*)q + 1 points at the 0 and (char*)q + 2 at the c, so the output is 0, c.

steps.title: Struct layout and what a pointer cast changes
steps.body: The members of a struct sit in memory one after another in the order they are declared. Here x, y, z are three chars, one byte each, at offsets 0, 1, 2 from the start of the struct. A pointer's type decides how far +1 moves: it moves by the size of the type pointed to. (char*)q reinterprets the same address as a pointer to char, so + 1 moves one byte, not one whole struct. The cast binds tighter than +, so (char*)q + 1 is ((char*)q) + 1. And %c prints a char as the character itself, without quotes.

steps.title: The stored values
steps.body: p = {'1', '0', 'a'+2}: x is the character 1, y is the character 0, and z is 'a' + 2. A character is its ASCII code in arithmetic, so 'a' + 2 = 97 + 2 = 99, which is 'c'.

steps.title: Evaluate the two arguments
steps.body: *((char*)q + 1) reads the byte at offset 1, y = '0'. *((char*)q + 2) reads the byte at offset 2, z = 'c'. The format "%c, %c" prints 0, then a comma and a space, then c: 0, c. That is option A.

shortcut.body: Bytes 1 and 2 of the struct are '0' and 'a'+2 = 'c'. %c prints bare characters, so the quotes in options C and D cannot appear. The output is 0, c.

traps.text: (B) 0, a+2: treating 'a'+2 as text. It is arithmetic on the character code: 97 + 2 = 99, the character c.
(C) '0', 'a+2': expecting the quotes and the expression to be printed. %c prints only the character, and the quotes belong to the C source, not to the output.
(D) '0', 'c': getting the value right but printing the source quotes. printf("%c, %c") writes 0, c with no quotes.

recognize.clues: A struct of three chars accessed through a pointer cast to char*, with offsets 1 and 2 added: reading individual bytes of the struct.
recognize.contrast: Without the cast, q+1 would step past the whole struct. The cast to char* makes the step one byte, which lands on the next member.

check.body: Check the stored value of z independently: the letter a has code 97, so a+2 has code 99, which is the letter c. The format has no quotes, so the printed text has only the two characters and a comma and space, which rules out every option with quote marks or the literal text a+2.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

The output of this program is _____.

solutionDiagram.alt: The call chain calc(4,81), calc(4,27), calc(4,9), calc(4,3) with the counter reaching 1, 2, 3, 4; calc(4,3) hits b == 3 and stops, so counter is 4.

steps.title: A global counter counts calls
steps.body: A global variable exists for the whole run and every call reads and writes the same one. Here calc runs counter++ as its very first statement, so counter ends up equal to the number of calls made to calc. Recursion stops at the base case, the branch that does not call calc again: b == 3. The values returned never touch counter, so the answer depends only on how many calls happen.

steps.title: Follow b down to the base case
steps.body: calc(4, 81) calls calc(4, 81/3 = 27), which calls calc(4, 9), which calls calc(4, 3). At b = 3 the base case returns 4*4*4 and makes no more calls. The calls were b = 81, 27, 9, 3: four calls, so counter = 4. The cubes on the way back (c*c*c) change the returned value and nothing else.

steps.title: Print
steps.body: main ignores the returned value and prints counter, which is 4.

shortcut.body: Calls = how many times 81 can be divided by 3 before reaching 3, plus the first call: 81 = 3^4 gives 4 calls. Counting the divisions (3) is the common slip.

traps.text: 3: counting the divisions by 3 (81 to 27 to 9 to 3) and forgetting that the very first call also executes counter++.
5: running the recursion down to b = 1. The base case is b == 3, so there is no call with b = 1.

recognize.clues: A global counter incremented at the top of a recursive function, with the second argument divided by 3 each call: the output counts calls, not values.
recognize.contrast: The returned cubes are a distraction. Only the number of calls matters, and it equals the number of terms in the chain 81, 27, ..., not the number of divisions.

check.body: Use the exponent: the chain divides by 3 each time until the argument is 3, so the arguments are the powers 3^4, 3^3, 3^2, 3^1. Each power is one call, which gives 4 entries, and the call with 3^1 is the base case that makes no further call.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program:

The output of the program above is

solutionDiagram.alt: Two pointer diagrams. After fun1, str1 still points to Hi and str2 to Bye because only copies were swapped. After fun2, the arrows cross: str1 points to Bye and str2 to Hi. Output Hi Bye Bye Hi.

steps.title: Call by value, and pointers to pointers
steps.body: C passes every argument by value: the function gets a copy. A char* variable holds the address of the first character of a string; "Hi" lives in memory once, and str1 holds its address. If a function receives a copy of that address, swapping the copies does nothing to the caller's variables. To change the caller's pointer variable itself, pass its address (a char**), and write through it with *. The rule: to change the variable, pass its address.

steps.title: fun1(str1, str2)
steps.body: s1 and s2 are copies of the two addresses. tmp = s1; s1 = s2; s2 = tmp swaps the copies. When fun1 returns they vanish, and str1 still points to "Hi", str2 to "Bye". The first printf prints "Hi Bye " (with a trailing space).

steps.title: fun2(&str1, &str2)
steps.body: Now s1 holds the address of the variable str1 and s2 the address of str2. *s1 is str1 itself. tmp = *s1; *s1 = *s2; *s2 = tmp swaps the contents of str1 and str2. After the call str1 points to "Bye" and str2 to "Hi", and the second printf prints "Bye Hi". The whole output is Hi Bye Bye Hi, option A.

shortcut.body: First call passes values: no effect, so Hi Bye. Second call passes addresses: swap, so Bye Hi. Total Hi Bye Bye Hi. If fun2 had also failed to swap you would get B, so the char** is the whole point.

traps.text: (B) Hi Bye Hi Bye: treating fun2 like fun1, as if the second call also swapped only copies. It receives addresses of str1 and str2, so it does swap them.
(C) Bye Hi Hi Bye: assuming fun1 really swaps str1 and str2 and that fun2 then swaps them back. fun1 swaps only local copies.
(D) Bye Hi Bye Hi: assuming fun1 swaps the caller's pointers and fun2 changes nothing, the reverse of what happens.

recognize.clues: Two functions with the same swap body, one taking char * and the other char **, and a printf after each call. The only difference is how many stars the parameters carry.
recognize.contrast: Swapping the pointed-to characters would need strcpy or element-wise copies; here only the pointer variables are swapped, so a pointer to the pointer is what gives the function access.

check.body: Replace the strings by plain ints, so fun1 becomes the familiar swap(int a, int b) that fails and fun2 becomes swap(int *a, int *b) that works. The same pass/fail split must appear, so the first printf shows no change and the second shows a swap.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C code. Assume that unsigned long int type length is 64 bits.

The value returned when we call fun with the input $2^{40}$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: First loop: i = 2^40 halves 40 times to reach 1, so j = 40. Second loop: j = 40, 20, 10, 5, 2 each add 1 to sum, then j = 1 stops, so sum = 5.

steps.title: Integer halving counts bits
steps.body: Integer division by 2 drops the remainder, so n/2 is the same as shifting right one bit. A loop that halves a number until it reaches 1 runs floor(log2 n) times: the number of halvings needed to go from n down to 1. In for (init; test; update) the test is checked before each pass, so a pass runs only while the test holds. The rule: count the halvings.

steps.title: First loop: j = 40
steps.body: i starts at n = 2^40 and each pass halves it while i > 1: 2^40, 2^39, ..., 2^1 are 40 values, each running one pass. Then i = 2^0 = 1 and the loop stops. So j = 40. A 64-bit unsigned long holds 2^40, so nothing overflows.

steps.title: Second loop: sum counts halvings of j
steps.body: Starting at j = 40 the passes run with j = 40, 20, 10, 5, 2, each with j > 1, adding 1 to sum each time. Then j = 2/2 = 1 and the loop ends (5/2 is 2 with the remainder dropped). sum = 5, option B.

shortcut.body: The function returns floor(log2(floor(log2 n))). For n = 2^40: log2 n = 40, then floor(log2 40) = 5 because 2^5 = 32 <= 40 < 64. No simulation needed.

traps.text: (A) 4: stopping the second loop one pass early, for example not counting the pass with j = 2. The pass runs because 2 > 1.
(C) 6: rounding log2 40 = 5.32 up to 6. Each pass needs j > 1, which gives the floor, not the ceiling.
(D) 40: returning the first loop count j rather than the number of halvings of j. The function returns sum, not j.

recognize.clues: Two for loops in a row, each with i = i/2 or j = j/2 and a test against 1, and the input given as a power of two. The second loop starts from the count left by the first.
recognize.contrast: A loop that adds a constant each pass (i = i + 2) runs about n/2 times; only repeated halving gives a logarithmic count.

check.body: Test the same function on a tiny input where tracing is easy: n = 4 gives j = 2 and then one pass, so sum = 1, matching floor(log2(log2 4)) = 1. The formula floor(log2(floor(log2 n))) therefore holds on a case small enough to simulate by hand.

questions.stem:
Consider the following program written in pseudo-code. Assume that x and y are integers.

The number of times that the print statement is executed by the call Count(1024,1024) is _____.

solutionDiagram.alt: One round: x runs 1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 and prints ten stars, then y drops by one and a new round starts. The rounds run for y = 1024 down to 2, which is 1023 rounds; 10 x 1023 = 10230 stars.

steps.title: Each call makes at most one more call
steps.body: Here every call of Count either stops or makes exactly one further call, so the calls form a single chain and the program is a loop in disguise. Count the prints by finding the repeating pattern. Rule of the program: while y != 1, a call with x != 1 prints one star and halves x; a call with x == 1 lowers y by 1 and restarts x at 1024.

steps.title: One round: 10 stars
steps.body: With y fixed (not 1), x goes 1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 by halving. The calls with x = 1024 down to 2 each print one star: that is 10 stars (2^10 = 1024 takes ten halvings). The call with x = 1 prints nothing; it goes to the else branch.

steps.title: How many rounds
steps.body: The else branch lowers y by one and restarts the round with x = 1024. The rounds start with y = 1024, 1023, ..., 2. When y has become 1 the outer test y != 1 fails and the call does nothing. That is 1023 rounds, each printing 10 stars.

shortcut.body: Stars = (halvings of 1024 to 1) times (values of y from 1024 down to 2) = 10 x 1023 = 10230. The only trap is whether the last y counts; it does not, because the test y != 1 fails first.

traps.text: 10240: using 1024 rounds. The rounds stop as soon as y reaches 1, so only y = 1024 down to 2, which is 1023 rounds, print.
11253: counting 11 prints per round by including the call with x = 1. That call takes the else branch and prints nothing.
10: stopping after one round, forgetting that the else branch restarts Count(1024, y) with a smaller y.

recognize.clues: A pseudo-code function that halves x while printing, and on x == 1 lowers y and restarts x at 1024. The question asks for a count of prints, not an output value.
recognize.contrast: A branching recursion such as Fibonacci needs a recurrence for the call count; this single-chain recursion needs only a product of loop-like counts.

check.body: Shrink the constants and trace by hand: Count(4,3) prints 2 stars at y = 3 and 2 at y = 2, then stops at y = 1, which is 2 x (3 - 1) = 4. The same pattern of halvings times (y - 1) rounds gives the count for the large input.

questions.stem: Match the following:

rows: (i) Sequence of memory locations to store addresses
(ii) A variable located in data section of memory
(iii) Request to allocate a CPU register to store data
(iv) A lost memory which cannot be freed

steps.title: Four C storage and memory ideas
steps.body: static on a variable gives it one fixed place for the whole run: a global-like slot in the data section of memory, not on the stack. malloc(n) reserves n bytes on the heap and returns their address; if the only variable holding that address is overwritten, the block can never be freed, a memory leak. char *ptr[10] declares an array of 10 pointers, so it is a sequence of memory locations that store addresses. register is a request to the compiler to keep the variable in a CPU register for speed; the compiler may ignore it.

steps.title: Match each line
steps.body: P: static char var; sits in the data section: (ii). Q: m = malloc(10); m = NULL; the ten bytes are still allocated but no pointer to them is left, a lost memory block that cannot be freed: (iv). R: char *ptr[10]; ten char pointers, a sequence of locations for addresses: (i). S: register int var1; a request to hold var1 in a CPU register: (iii).

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: P to (ii), Q to (iv), R to (i), S to (iii) is option A.

shortcut.body: Q must be (iv) (the leak) and S must be (iii) (register); only option A pairs those two correctly. Confirm P to (ii) and R to (i), and you are done in under a minute.

traps.text: (B) Q to (i), R to (iv): swapping malloc and the pointer array. The array of pointers is the sequence of address slots; the malloc then NULL is the loss.
(C) R to (iii), S to (i): swapping the pointer array and register. register asks for a CPU register, and an array of pointers needs memory.
(D) P to (iii), S to (ii): treating static as a register request. A static variable lives in the data section; register is the one that asks for a CPU register.

recognize.clues: A match-the-following question pairing code lines with storage descriptions: static, malloc followed by an overwritten pointer, an array of pointers, and register.
recognize.contrast: An array of pointers (char *ptr[10]) is itself a block of addresses, whereas a pointer to heap memory is a single address; do not mix the container with what it points to.

check.body: Check each pairing in reverse: read each description and confirm exactly one code line fits it. If two lines seem to fit one description, the pairing is wrong. A valid answer uses every description exactly once.

questions.stem:
Consider the following function implemented in C:

The output of invoking printxy(1,1) is

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of x, y and ptr after each statement of printxy(1,1): x = 0; then ptr = &x; then y = *ptr makes y 0; then *ptr = 1 makes x 1. The output is 1,0.

steps.title: Parameters are local variables; a pointer names a variable
steps.body: In C the parameters x and y of printxy are ordinary local variables that start as copies of the arguments, here both 1. &x is the address of the local x, and ptr = &x makes ptr point at it. Then *ptr is the variable x itself: reading *ptr gives the current value of x, and writing *ptr = v changes x. The statements run top to bottom, each storing into one variable.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: Start: x = 1, y = 1. x = 0 makes x = 0. ptr = &x points ptr at x. y = *ptr copies the current value of x, 0, into y, so y = 0. *ptr = 1 writes 1 into x, so x = 1. y stays 0 because it was only a copy.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: printf prints x, y = 1,0. This is option C.

shortcut.body: The order matters: y = *ptr runs while x is 0, so y = 0; only afterwards *ptr = 1 sets x to 1. Output 1,0.

traps.text: (A) 0,0: forgetting that *ptr = 1 writes into x, the variable ptr points at. After that statement x is 1, not 0.
(B) 0,1: ignoring both pointer statements, so x stays 0 and y stays 1. y = *ptr copies 0 into y, and *ptr = 1 sets x.
(D) 1,1: leaving y at its argument value. y = *ptr overwrites y with 0 before x becomes 1.

recognize.clues: The parameters x and y are reassigned inside the function and a pointer is aimed at the parameter x. The printed values come from the local copies, not from the caller.
recognize.contrast: Passing &x from the caller would change the caller variable; here the address is of the callee own parameter, so the caller is unaffected either way.

check.body: Rerun the trace with different call arguments such as printxy(5, 9). Because x = 0 is executed first, the starting values of the parameters are overwritten or unused, and the printed pair must come out the same. If it did not, a step of the trace read a stale value.

questions.stem:
Consider the C program fragment below which is meant to divide x by y using repeated subtractions. The variables x, y, q and r are all unsigned int.

Which of the following conditions on the variables x, y, q and r before the execution of the fragment will ensure that the loop terminates in a state satisfying the condition x == (y*q + r)?

solutionDiagram.alt: Table trying each option on a start state: A (5,1,0,0) ends with 5 != 0, B (1,1,1,1) ends with 1 != 2, D (0,1,0,1) ends with 0 != 1, and C (7,3,0,7) ends at q = 2, r = 1 where 7 = 3*2 + 1.

steps.title: Loop invariant and termination
steps.body: A loop invariant is a statement that is true before the loop starts and that each pass of the body keeps true; then it is also true when the loop ends. Here the statement is x == y*q + r. The loop ends in that state if three things hold: the statement is true before the loop, each pass preserves it, and the loop terminates. Unsigned variables never go negative, and the test r >= y is checked before each pass.

steps.title: The body preserves y*q + r
steps.body: One pass sets r to r - y and q to q + 1. The new value y(q + 1) + (r - y) = yq + r is the old value. So if x == y*q + r before the loop, it is true after every pass and when the loop ends. Termination: if y > 0, each pass lowers r by y, so r must drop below y after finitely many passes. If y = 0 then r >= 0 is always true and the loop runs forever.

steps.title: Which option sets this up
steps.body: We need the invariant true at the start and y > 0. (A) q == r and r == 0 gives y*0 + 0 = 0, so x == 0 is needed too, not promised: x = 5, y = 1 fails. (B) r == x with y > 0 but q free: y*q + x equals x only when q = 0, so q = 1, y = 1, x = 1 ends with 2. (D) q == 0 and y > 0 but r is free: x = 0, y = 1, r = 1 ends with 1 while x = 0. (C) q == 0 and r == x gives y*0 + x = x, true at the start, with y > 0 for termination. Answer C.

shortcut.body: The target equation x == y*q + r is the invariant. To make it true at the start without extra assumptions you need q == 0 and r == x, and y > 0 to stop the loop: only option C. Unsafe only if y might be 0.

traps.text: (A) q == r && r == 0 says nothing about x or y. With x = 5, y = 1 the loop does not run and x == y*0 + 0 is false.
(B) fixes r == x and y > 0 but leaves q free. A nonzero q, such as q = 1 with x = y = 1, breaks the equation from the start.
(D) fixes q == 0 and y > 0 but leaves r free, so x == y*0 + r may be false at the start, for example x = 0 and r = 1.

recognize.clues: A while loop that subtracts y from r and adds 1 to q, and a target equation x == y*q + r that must hold at exit. The question asks which entry conditions guarantee it.
recognize.contrast: A termination argument is separate from the invariant: the invariant gives the equation at exit, while y > 0 is what makes the loop actually exit.

check.body: Check the surviving option on an actual run: x = 7, y = 3, q = 0, r = 7 passes twice and ends with q = 2, r = 1, and 3*2 + 1 = 7. Then check each rejected option with a counterexample so that every wrong choice has been seen to fail.

questions.stem:
Consider the following snippet of a C program. Assume that swap(&x, &y) exchanges the contents of x and y.

The output of the program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The array after each sweep: start 3 5 1 4 6 2; pass 1 forward 5 3 4 6 2 1; pass 1 backward 6 5 3 4 2 1; pass 2 forward 6 5 4 3 2 1; the later sweeps change nothing. array[3], the fourth cell, is 3.

steps.title: What the loops do
steps.body: The while loop keeps going until done stays 1, which means a whole pass made no swap. The first for loop swaps neighbours when the left one is smaller than the right one, pushing small values to the right. The second for loop, run backwards, swaps when array[i] > array[i-1], pulling large values to the left. This is bubble sort in both directions, ordering the array from largest to smallest. When a full pass changes nothing, no neighbouring pair is in increasing order, so the array is in descending order.

steps.title: Trace the passes
steps.body: Start 3 5 1 4 6 2. Pass 1 forward gives 5 3 4 6 2 1: swaps at i = 0 (3,5), 2 (1,4), 3 (1,6), 4 (1,2). Pass 1 backward gives 6 5 3 4 2 1: swaps at i = 3 (4,6), 2 (3,6), 1 (5,6). Pass 2 forward swaps (3,4) and gives 6 5 4 3 2 1, and the backward sweep changes nothing. Pass 3 swaps nothing, so done stays 1 and the loop exits.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The final array is 6 5 4 3 2 1 and array[3] is 3.

shortcut.body: Skip the trace: the loop exits only when no neighbours are in increasing order, so the array is sorted in descending order, 6 5 4 3 2 1. array[3] is the fourth largest value, 3. Safe because every swap removes an out-of-order pair, so the loop does end.

traps.text: 4: stopping after the first full pass (6 5 3 4 2 1), or sorting in ascending order, where index 3 of 1 2 3 4 5 6 is 4. The swap condition array[i] < array[i+1] sorts downwards.
6: reading array[3] after the first forward sweep (5 3 4 6 2 1) instead of after the loop has finished.

recognize.clues: A done flag that is reset to 0 on every swap, and two for loops sweeping in opposite directions with a comparison between array[i] and its neighbour. The output is a single array element.
recognize.contrast: A single-direction bubble sort and this two-way version end in the same sorted array; only the number of passes differs, which is why tracing every pass is unnecessary.

check.body: Check by counting, which is independent of the trace: in descending order, array[3] has exactly three values larger than it. In 3 5 1 4 6 2 the values larger than 3 are 5, 4 and 6, three of them, so 3 sits at index 3. Ascending order would instead put the value with three smaller ones there, which is 4, and the swap test array[i] < array[i+1] rules that direction out.

Consider the following C Program.

The output of the program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table of m, n and n1 after each statement: n = ++m gives m=11, n=11; n1 = m++ gives n1=11, m=12; n-- makes n 10; --n1 makes n1 10; n -= n1 makes n 0, which is printed.

steps.title: Prefix and postfix increment
steps.body: Both ++m and m++ add 1 to m. The difference is the value of the expression: ++m (prefix) is the value after the increment, m++ (postfix) is the value before it. The same holds for -- on n and n1. Each statement here changes each variable at most once, so the result is well defined. The rule: prefix gives the new value, postfix gives the old.

steps.title: Step through
steps.body: m = 10. n = ++m: m becomes 11 and n = 11. n1 = m++: n1 takes the old value 11, then m becomes 12. n--: n = 10. --n1: n1 = 10. n -= n1 means n = n - n1 = 10 - 10 = 0.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: printf prints n, which is 0.

shortcut.body: Both n and n1 end at 10 (each was 11 and was decremented once), so n - n1 = 0. The increments of m do not matter beyond the values copied out.

traps.text: -1: reading n1 = m++ as giving the incremented value 12, so n1 = 11 after --n1 and n = 10 - 11.
1: forgetting that n-- lowers n from 11 to 10, so n - n1 = 11 - 10 = 1.

recognize.clues: The mix of ++m and m++ on the right-hand side of assignments, followed by n-- and --n1 as separate statements. Every variable is modified once per statement.
recognize.contrast: Expressions like m++ + ++m modify one variable twice between sequence points and are undefined; here each statement stands alone, so a plain trace is valid.

check.body: Check with a second route: after the assignments the two copies differ from m by the operators used, and the later decrements shift both by the same amount. Rewrite the statements without the operators, using plain m = m + 1 and temporary copies, and confirm the final difference is the same.

Consider the following C Program.

The output of the program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: The string GATECSIT2017 with indices 0 to 12. 2[p] is T (84) and 6[p] is I (73), so c + 84 - 73 - 1 = c + 10, which points at the character 1; the remaining string 17 has length 2.

steps.title: Strings, indexing and pointer sums
steps.body: A C string is an array of chars ending with a zero byte, written \0 and not counted by strlen. strlen(s) counts the characters before that zero byte. The expression a[i] is defined as *(a + i), and since a + i equals i + a, writing i[a] means exactly the same thing: 2[p] is p[2]. A char used in arithmetic is its ASCII code, so 'T' is 84 and 'I' is 73. Pointer plus integer moves that many chars along the string.

steps.title: Index the string
steps.body: "GATECSIT2017" has indices G0 A1 T2 E3 C4 S5 I6 T7 2(8) 0(9) 1(10) 7(11), 12 characters. So 2[p] = p[2] = 'T' = 84 and 6[p] = p[6] = 'I' = 73.

steps.title: Evaluate the pointer
steps.body: c + 2[p] - 6[p] - 1 is c + 84 - 73 - 1 = c + 10, evaluated left to right. c + 10 points at index 10, the character 1 of "17". strlen of that suffix counts 2 characters before the terminator.

shortcut.body: The offset is (T - I) - 1 = 11 - 1 = 10, since T is 11 letters after I in the alphabet. strlen = 12 - 10 = 2. Unsafe only if the string had been read as a different length: count it carefully.

traps.text: 12: ignoring the offset and taking strlen of the whole string. The pointer is moved forward by 10.
10: confusing the offset with the length. c + 10 is where the suffix starts; the suffix length is 12 - 10.
1: forgetting the - 1, which puts the pointer at c + 11 and leaves only the character 7.

recognize.clues: The odd form 2[p] and 6[p] on a char pointer, and the string passed to strlen as c plus an offset made from character codes. It is a string-indexing and pointer-offset question in disguise.
recognize.contrast: It is not a pure pointer-arithmetic question about element sizes: here the offset comes from character values, so the ASCII codes decide how far the pointer moves.

check.body: Redo the offset from letter positions, with no ASCII codes: T is the 20th letter and I the 9th, a gap of 11, and minus 1 gives 10. At the edges, an offset of 12 would leave 0 characters and an offset of 11 would leave 1, so offset 10 leaves 12 - 10 = 2.

Consider the following C code:

The code suffers from which one of the following problems:
options: compiler error as the return of malloc is not typecast appropriately
compiler error because the comparison should be made as x == NULL and not as shown
compiles successfully but execution may result in dangling pointer
compiles successfully but execution may result in memory leak

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: x points to heap block A holding 0. Right: after the second malloc x points to block B holding 10 and block A, drawn dashed, has no pointer to it, so it is leaked.

steps.title: The words the options use
steps.body: The heap is the region of memory from which malloc hands out blocks at run time. A block stays reserved until the program passes its address to free. A pointer variable such as x is only a small box on the stack that stores the address of a block. A memory leak is a heap block that is still reserved but that no pointer in the program holds any more, so it can never be freed. A dangling pointer is the opposite situation: a pointer that still holds the address of a block that has already been freed, and is then used. The rule that decides this question: every malloc must be matched by a free of the same address, and overwriting the only pointer to a block before freeing it leaks the block.

steps.title: Rule out the two compiler-error options
steps.body: In C a void * (what malloc returns) converts to any object pointer type without a cast, so the cast in option A is optional and its absence is no error. The comparison NULL == x is a legal expression that is true exactly when x == NULL is true; writing the constant first is a style that catches a mistyped single =, and it compiles. So the code compiles, and options A and B are out.

steps.title: Follow the pointer and the heap blocks
steps.body: The first malloc gives block A and x holds its address. assignval(x, 0) stores 0 into A (*x = val) and returns the same address, so x still points to A. Now if (x) tests the pointer, not the stored value, and the pointer is not NULL (we returned earlier if it were), so the condition is true although A holds 0. Inside the if, malloc gives block B and the assignment x = ... overwrites the only pointer to A. After x = assignval(x, 10), block B holds 10 and x points to B.

steps.title: End of main
steps.body: printf prints *x, which is 10. free(x) releases block B. Block A was never passed to free and no variable holds its address, so it stays reserved until the process ends: a memory leak. Nothing is used after being freed, because the only free is the last use of x, so there is no dangling pointer. The answer is option D.

shortcut.body: Count mallocs and frees on the path that runs. Two mallocs execute (if (x) is true for any valid pointer) and only one free(x) runs, on the second block. One block is unfreed and unreachable, so it leaks. The two compile-error options are false in C, which settles it in about 40 seconds.

traps.text: Casting the result of malloc is a C++ requirement, not a C one. In C the void * converts implicitly, so omitting the cast compiles.
NULL == x and x == NULL mean the same thing, and the first form is legal. Nothing in the language demands the variable on the left.
A dangling pointer needs a use after free. Here x is freed at the very end and never read again. The real defect is the opposite: block A was never freed.
Reading if (x) as "if the stored value is non-zero" and concluding the branch is skipped because assignval stored 0. The test is on the pointer, which is non-NULL, so the second malloc runs.

recognize.clues: Two malloc calls assign to the same pointer x, and only one free(x) appears at the end. The options name compile errors, a dangling pointer and a leak, which are the standard dynamic-memory defects.
recognize.contrast: A dangling pointer needs a use after free; a leak needs a lost address with no free. Here nothing is read after the free, but one block loses its only pointer.

check.body: Follow the first address by itself. After the second malloc result is stored in x, the only free receives x, which is the second address. The first address is never an argument to free and no variable holds it, so that block cannot be released.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two functions.

The output printed when fun1(5) is called is

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain of calls fun1(5), fun2(3), fun1(4), fun2(2), fun1(3), fun2(1), fun1(2), fun2(0) with the value each call prints before its inner call, the value of n at the end, and the value it prints after the inner call returns.

steps.title: What recursion with a print on each side does
steps.body: A call is a function running with its own private copy of its parameter n. Each function here prints n, calls the other function, and when that call returns, prints n again. So every call produces two prints: one on the way in (before the inner call) and one on the way out (after it). The inner call runs to completion first, so the "after" prints appear in the reverse order of the calls. Two rules decide the output: each call has its own n, and ++n in fun2 changes that call's own n before the "after" print reads it.

steps.title: Go in: the "before" prints
steps.body: fun1(5) prints 5 and calls fun2(5-2) = fun2(3). fun2(3) prints 3 and calls fun1(++n); ++n makes this n equal to 4, so the call is fun1(4). fun1(4) prints 4 and calls fun2(2). fun2(2) prints 2, makes n 3, calls fun1(3). fun1(3) prints 3 and calls fun2(1). fun2(1) prints 1, makes n 2, calls fun1(2). fun1(2) prints 2 and calls fun2(0), which returns at once without printing (n == 0). The before prints are 5, 3, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2.

steps.title: Come out: the "after" prints
steps.body: Now the calls return from the innermost one. fun1(2) prints its n = 2. fun2(1) prints its n, which ++n changed from 1 to 2, so it prints 2. fun1(3) prints 3. fun2(2) has n = 3 after ++n, so it prints 3. fun1(4) prints 4. fun2(3) has n = 4 after ++n, so it prints 4. fun1(5) prints 5. The after prints are 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5.

steps.title: Join the two halves
steps.body: Writing the before prints then the after prints gives 5342312 followed by 2233445, which is 53423122233445. This is option A. A 0 is never printed because both functions return at n == 0 before their first printf.

shortcut.body: Options B and D contain a 0, which can never be printed (both functions return before printing when n is 0), so cross them out. A and C differ in the second half: the middle of the after prints comes from fun2, whose n was increased by ++n. fun2(1) then prints 2, not 1, so the tail starts 2 2 and not 2 1: option A. About 1.5 minutes. The shortcut fails if you forget that ++n changes n for the later printf.

traps.text: This answer contains 0 in the tail. Both functions test n == 0 and return before printing, so no 0 is ever printed.

This is what you get if the "after" print in fun2 shows the value n had on entry (1, 2, 3) instead of the incremented value (2, 3, 4). ++n changes the same variable, so the later printf sees the new value.
Also contains a 0, which no call prints. The reversed-looking tail comes from mixing up the order in which the after prints happen.

recognize.clues: Two functions that call each other, a printf before and after the inner call, and a pre-increment ++n inside one of them. All three features affect the order or the value printed.
recognize.contrast: This is not tail recursion: the work after the inner call matters, so the output has a mirrored second half rather than a single pass.

check.body: Check the tail by pairs. A fun2 call that entered with m prints m + 1 afterwards, because of ++n, and the fun1 call it made entered with m + 1 and prints m + 1. The pairs are (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4), then 5, so the tail is 2233445. Option A ends in 2233445; option C ends in 2132435.

questions.stem:
Consider the C functions foo and bar given below:

Invocations of foo(3) and bar(3) will result in :
options: Infinite loop and abnormal termination respectively.
Abnormal termination and infinite loop respectively.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: foo(3) calls foo(3) again and again so frames pile up until the stack overflows. Right: bar(3), bar(2), bar(1), bar(0) returns 0, then bar(1) loops and calls bar(0) forever at constant depth.

steps.title: Two ways a function can never finish
steps.body: Each call to a function gets a stack frame holding its own parameters and local variables. A function that calls itself forever with no call ever returning keeps adding frames; the stack is a fixed-size region, so it runs out and the program is killed: a stack overflow, which the exam calls abnormal termination. A function that keeps repeating a loop at the same depth, adding no frames, runs for ever without crashing: an infinite loop. The rule to apply: look at the argument passed in the recursive call to see whether the recursion gets closer to a base case, then look at whether the loop test can ever become false.

steps.title: foo(3): the argument never shrinks
steps.body: In foo the call is foo(val--). Post-decrement hands the callee the old value 3 and lowers the caller's own val to 2 before the call starts; the callee's val is 3 again. So foo(3) calls foo(3), which calls foo(3), and so on. The argument stays 3, the inner call never gets closer to val being 0, and no call returns before its inner call does. Frames pile up until the stack overflows. foo(3) ends in abnormal termination.

steps.title: bar(3): the recursion ends but the loop does not
steps.body: In bar the argument is val - 1, so bar(3) calls bar(2), which calls bar(1), which calls bar(0). bar(0) skips its while loop (0 > 0 is false) and returns 0. Back in bar(1), the call has returned but val in bar(1) was never changed: it is still 1, so the test val > 0 is true again and bar(1) calls bar(0) once more, and again, for ever. The depth stays at 4 frames, so the stack never overflows; the program loops without end. bar(3) is an infinite loop.

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.body: foo: abnormal termination. bar: infinite loop. That is "Abnormal termination and infinite loop respectively", option C.

shortcut.body: In each function the loop variable val is never changed inside bar, and inside foo the post-decrement lowers only the caller's copy, so the callee still receives the old value. Ask two questions: does the argument shrink (foo no, so unbounded depth, crash; bar yes, so recursion ends) and does the loop test change (bar no, so it spins). 1.5 minutes. Unsafe only if you read foo(val--) as foo(val - 1).

traps.text: Assuming the code sums something and returns 6 = 3 + 2 + 1. Neither function ever reaches its return statement: the loop test never fails.

The two behaviours swapped. Candidates see val-- and think the value decreases, so foo seems to terminate or loop, while the unchanged val in bar is missed. Post-decrement passes the old value, so foo recurses without end; bar never changes its own val, so it spins.
bar never grows its stack: its call depth stays at 4, so it cannot overflow. It just loops, which is not abnormal termination.

recognize.clues: A while loop wrapped around a recursive call, with val-- in one function and val - 1 in the other. The question is how each one fails to terminate.
recognize.contrast: Infinite recursion and an infinite loop look alike but differ in stack use: only the first keeps adding frames and crashes. Telling them apart means checking whether the call depth grows.

check.body: Re-enter the frames by hand. In bar, once bar(0) returns, the frame of bar(1) still has val equal to 1, so its test val > 0 is true again and the same call repeats from the same state. In foo, every call receives 3, because val-- passes the old value, so the argument sequence 3, 3, 3, ... never reaches a base case.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C program.

Recall that strlen is defined in string.h as returning a value of type size_t, which is an unsigned int. The output of the program is ____________.

steps.title: Signed and unsigned subtraction
steps.body: An unsigned integer type holds only values 0 and above, and arithmetic on it is done modulo 2^N, where N is its number of bits: a result that would be negative wraps around to a very large number. A signed int holds negative values normally. The rule that decides this question: when both operands of - are unsigned, the result is unsigned, and so a "negative" difference becomes a huge positive number, which is greater than 0. The comparison > c is therefore true for every difference except exactly 0.

steps.title: Compute the lengths
steps.body: strlen("abc") = 3 and strlen("defgh") = 5. Both are of type size_t, which is unsigned, so strlen(s) - strlen(t) is 3 - 5 evaluated in unsigned arithmetic: it wraps to 2^N - 2 (about 4.29 billion on a 32-bit size_t), not -2.

steps.title: Evaluate the condition and the output
steps.body: c is an unsigned int equal to 0, and 2^N - 2 > 0 is true. So the conditional expression takes the first branch: len = strlen(s) = 3. printf prints 3. The answer is 3.

shortcut.body: Spot size_t in the note: it tells you the subtraction is unsigned. Any unsigned difference of two unequal numbers is greater than 0, so the test is true and the program prints strlen(s) = 3. 1 minute. If strlen returned a signed int, the test 3 - 5 > 0 would be false and the answer would be 5.

traps.text: Answering 5. That is the result if the difference is treated as the signed value -2, so that -2 > 0 is false and the second branch gives strlen(t). The question note about size_t is there to prevent exactly this.
Answering -2 or 2, i.e. printing the difference. The program never prints the difference; it only uses it in a comparison, and the printed value is a length.

recognize.clues: The note that strlen returns an unsigned size_t, and a difference of two lengths compared with an unsigned c. The signedness of the subtraction decides the comparison.
recognize.contrast: With signed ints the same code would see a negative difference and take the other branch. The unsigned type is what makes the test true for any unequal pair.

check.body: Test the boundary where the two lengths are equal. The difference is then 0 in either reading, the test is false, and the program prints strlen(t). Any unequal pair makes the unsigned difference nonzero, hence greater than 0, which is why 3 and 5 take the first branch and print strlen(s) = 3.

questions.stem: The output of executing the following C program is ____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Table for i = 5 down to 1: the binary form of i, the number of 1-bits added to the static count, the count after the call, the value returned and the running value of x, ending at 23.

steps.title: Static local variables and bit operations
steps.body: A local variable declared static is created and initialised once, before the program starts, and keeps its value between calls: static int count = 0 runs once, not at every call. An ordinary local would be reset on each call. Two bit operations are used: v & 1 is 1 when the lowest bit of v is 1 and 0 otherwise, and v >>= 1 shifts v right by one place, dropping the lowest bit. The loop therefore adds the number of 1-bits of v to count. The rule: total(v) adds popcount(v) to a count that carries over, and returns the running total, not popcount(v).

steps.title: Per call: count after each call
steps.body: Popcounts: 5 = 101 has 2 ones, 4 = 100 has 1, 3 = 11 has 2, 2 = 10 has 1, 1 = 1 has 1. count starts at 0 and only grows. total(5) returns 2. total(4) returns 2 + 1 = 3. total(3) returns 3 + 2 = 5. total(2) returns 5 + 1 = 6. total(1) returns 6 + 1 = 7.

steps.title: Accumulate into x
steps.body: x is also static but only main uses it; it starts at 0. The loop runs for i = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and adds each returned value: 2, then 5, then 10, then 16, then 23. printf prints 23.

shortcut.body: Write the running count after each call (2, 3, 5, 6, 7), as running popcounts of 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, then add them: 2 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 23. About 2 minutes. A common check: the last return is 7, the total number of 1-bits of 5 to 1.

traps.text: Answering 7, the last value total returns (the total number of 1-bits in 5, 4, 3, 2, 1). x does not hold that count: it adds the running count returned by every call, 2 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 7.

Answering 7 for a different reason: assuming count is reset to 0 on each call (as for an ordinary local). Then the returns would be 2, 1, 2, 1, 1 and x would be 7. static makes count persist, so the returns are 2, 3, 5, 6, 7.

recognize.clues: static int count inside total, called repeatedly from a loop in main, with a bit-counting while loop. Persistence of count across calls is the whole point.
recognize.contrast: An ordinary local would restart at 0 on each call and return the plain 1-bit count. Static storage makes the returns accumulate instead.

check.body: Cross-check the last return: after all five calls count must equal the total number of 1-bits of 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1. Add the five bit counts and compare with the last returned value in your table.

A static local variable is initialised once and keeps its value between calls. The expression v & 1 reads the lowest bit and v >>= 1 drops it.
The loop adds the number of 1-bits of v to count. Since count persists, each call returns the running total so far.
Make a row for each value of i in the order the loop uses. Fill in the 1-bit count, the running count after the call, and the new x.
The first call, with i = 5, adds two 1-bits and returns 2, so x becomes 2. Carry count forward from there.
